items.name: Pivot Practice
items.setup: Two footholds and two handholds.
steps: Reach as high as you can with one arm without moving anything else.
Then stay on the holds and pivot the feet (turn in or out) and reach again.
items.why: Shows how turning the hips adds reach.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: big holds.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Clockwork
items.setup: A large multi-directional hold (or a cluster of holds facing different ways).
steps: Move through several hand and body positions on the one hold before going to the finish.
Hold Recycler: set a problem that forces using one hold several ways.
items.why: Practises reading hold direction and moving the body to match it.
items.variations: On a spray wall for Ages 14+.
items.risk: Low hold.

items.name: Balanced Flag
items.setup: A tape mark, balance pod or marker on the ground for each climber.
steps: Stand on one foot and flag the other out to the side.
Time your own hold.
Switch feet, then try to beat your own last time.
items.why: Off-the-wall introduction to how a flag balances the body, measured against your own last hold.
items.variations: Eyes closed for older kids.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Flag Boxes
items.setup: Colored tape on each shoe (right red, left blue) and matching tape on footholds.
steps: Climb a problem where each foot may only use holds of its color.
Flag when your foot has no hold.
items.why: Forces flagging decisions.
items.variations: Fewer taped holds for Ages 14+.
items.risk: Low problems.
coachingCues: A flag is a leg used for balance, not to support weight, often to stop a barn-door swing.
Normal flag: the free foot stays on the same side. Inside-flag: it crosses in front of the standing foot. Outside-flag: it crosses behind.
A back-step (outside edge of the shoe) often appears with a flag on the other leg.
commonMistakes: Trying to stand on the flagged foot, or flagging without moving the hips toward the standing foot.

progressions.easier: A taped box or volume to rest the flagged foot against on a gentle wall.
progressions.harder: The same flag on a slightly steeper problem where a barn-door is obvious without it.

images.alt: Climber in a back-step with the free leg flagged out to the side for balance, hips turned into the wall.

items.name: Step Flag Reach
items.setup: An easy route with plenty of holds.
steps: Follow the pattern step, flag, reach all the way up.
items.why: Repetition makes flagging automatic.
items.variations: Inside and outside flags.
items.risk: Top rope or low.

items.name: Monkey Tails
items.setup: An easy boulder or top-rope route.
steps: Climb the whole route with only one foot.
Use the other foot as a monkey tail, swinging it to keep balance.
items.why: Kids feel how a flag counterbalances.
items.variations: Switch feet next lap.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Team Reach Challenge
items.setup: Groups of two or three of similar height; set start hand and foot holds.
steps: Start on the holds and reach as far as you can using a flag.
Mark your own farthest hold.
Rest, then try to pass your own mark.
items.why: Shows how far a good flag extends reach. Note your own mark and try to pass it.
items.variations: Try both directions and keep the better of your own two marks.
items.risk: Low holds.

items.name: Heel and Toe
items.setup: An area with large holds.
steps: Use a heel or toe hook for 5–6 moves in a row.
Or traverse using only heel and toe hooks.
items.why: Builds confidence in hooks, which feel strange at first.
items.variations: Bat hangs with a close spot and a toy to pick up underneath.
items.risk: Bat hangs only with a coach spotting closely, low, over a clear mat.
coachingCues: A heel hook uses the back of the heel to press on a hold for balance or leverage.
A toe hook presses the top of the toes under a hold to pull the body in, often on overhangs.
Set the hook, then move the hips; a hook that is only hooked as an afterthought often pops.
commonMistakes: Hooking and then immediately cutting the other foot, before the hips have moved in.
Using a bat-hang (hanging upside down from the toes) when the lesson is an ordinary toe hook.

progressions.easier: A large, obvious heel hook on a volume or rail, standing height.
progressions.harder: A toe hook on a volume to keep the body into an overhang, with a planned landing.

equipment: Volumes or rails that accept a heel or toe

images.alt: Indoor heel hook: the back of the heel is set on a hold, with the free leg and body clearly visible.
Climber using a toe hook on a volume, the top of the shoe pressing under the hold to pull the body in.

items.name: Static and Dynamic
items.setup: A route 5.9 or easier, or 3–4 boulders.
steps: Climb it twice back to back.
First as statically as possible (lock off and hover).
Then as dynamically as possible.
items.why: Contrasts the two styles so climbers can choose.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: slow sloth and quick frog.
items.risk: Rest 2 minutes between problems.
coachingCues: Static: slow, controlled movement that keeps three points on.
A dyno is a jump or leap to an out-of-reach hold; missing it usually means a fall, so practice only on pads or a belay, from a height you have agreed.
A deadpoint is a more controlled dynamic: the hand arrives at the apex while the other contacts stay on.
commonMistakes: Jumping on a move that can be done statically, just because jumping feels exciting.
Practicing dynos over a gap in the pads.

progressions.easier: Do the same easy sequence once statically, then with one slightly more dynamic reach still in control.
progressions.harder: A short, padded dyno to a large hold, then compare it with a static version if one exists.

images.alt: Climber making a dynamic reach on a boulder, one foot off the rock, both hands going to a higher hold.

researchSources.title: Glossary: dyno, deadpoint, static rope (contrast with dynamic movement)

items.name: Setter for a Day
items.setup: A quiet or kids-only area; tape.
steps: Each kid (or pair) sets a problem with a set number of moves.
Others try it.
Tape the Movement: coaches pre-tape holds to force high steps, rock-overs or flags.
items.why: Setting teaches how holds force movement.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: four-move problems.
items.risk: Low problems only.

items.name: Any Feet One Color Hands
items.setup: Problems with taped handholds.
steps: Hands only on one color.
Feet on anything.
Progress to feet-follow-hands.
items.why: A stepping stone to following a full route.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big holds.
items.risk: Low problems.

items.name: Systems Wall Drills
items.setup: A systems wall; three climbers, one per color.
steps: Choose one hold type (pinches, slopers).
Two 20-second sets bumping hands, 10 seconds rest.
Speed version: matching holds, feet fixed.
items.why: Structured hold-type and movement practice.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): bumping only.
items.risk: Teens only, short sets, stop when form breaks.

items.name: Read and Point
items.setup: A route or problem the climber hasn't tried.
steps: Before touching the wall, point to each hand and foot hold in order and say the moves.
Climb it.
Afterwards, say what matched your plan and what changed.
items.why: Reading first saves energy and builds the onsight skill used in competitions.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: point to the next three holds only. Ages 14+: visualize with eyes closed and time the read like a comp observation period.
items.risk: Read from outside the fall zone of other climbers.
coachingCues: Point to each hand and foot in order before leaving the ground.
If they get stuck, come down, re-point, and try the same sequence again.
commonMistakes: Pointing only at handholds and ignoring feet.

progressions.easier: Coach and climber point together on a short problem.
progressions.harder: The climber points silently, then climbs; the partner checks whether the feet matched the plan.

equipment: A short boulder or route the group can see from the ground

researchSources.title: Add On / route reading (planning moves before leaving the ground)

items.name: Draw the Route
items.setup: Paper and pencils; a boulder or route.
steps: Give kids a set time to read a climb (shorter for experienced climbers).
They turn around and draw it from memory.
Compare drawings to the wall, then climb.
items.why: Sequence reading and memory; prepares climbers for comp observation.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: draw only the hand holds.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Guess the Grade
items.setup: An unfamiliar section of wall; sticky notes over the grade tags.
steps: Each kid guesses the grade after reading and/or climbing.
Reveal the grade and talk about what you noticed. There is no ranking.
items.why: Builds reading and stops grades from deciding whether kids try a climb.
items.variations: No Tag, No Problem: pick climbs from too far back to see grades.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Opposite Day
items.setup: An easy boulder; two colors of tape.
steps: Kids identify which holds are for the right hand and which for the left.
Mark them with two tape colors.
Climb it using right-hand holds with the left hand and vice versa.
items.why: Reading hand sequences and solving a familiar problem in a new way.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: three or four holds.
items.risk: Easy boulder.

items.name: Wrong Beta Only
items.setup: A climb with an obvious sequence.
steps: A coach or climber shows the intended beta.
Climbers find a completely different way to do it.
items.why: Easiest isn't the goal: exploring new movement grows the toolbox.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): change only one section.
items.risk: Stay on terrain well within ability.

items.name: The Beta
items.setup: A boulder problem; a coach on the wall.
steps: Climbers coach the coach through the problem with words.
The coach does exactly what they say, funny mistakes included.
items.why: Kids learn to read routes, communicate and think through problems together.
items.variations: Kids must use climbing vocabulary.
items.risk: Low problem; the coach chooses when to step off.

items.name: Beta Swap
items.setup: Pairs on the same project.
steps: Each climber tries the problem their own way.
Explain your beta to your partner.
Try your partner's beta and pick the best parts of each.
items.why: Height and style change the best beta; sharing builds problem-solving and respect.
items.variations: Ages 14+: film both and compare.
items.risk: Partners spot each other.

items.name: Observe Others Climbing
items.setup: A route or problem you just climbed.
steps: Watch an advanced climber on the same climb.
Note how they move, which footholds they use, and why.
Or watch World Cup videos for footwork details.
items.why: Watching skilled climbers gives a model to copy.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): write one footwork detail to try.
items.risk: Watch from outside fall zones.

items.name: Video Self-Review
items.setup: A phone on a stand (with permission per gym and family rules).
steps: Film an attempt.
Watch it once for feet, once for hips, once for breathing.
Pick one change for the next attempt.
items.why: Teens can see what they can't feel.
items.variations: Side-by-side with a partner's beta.
items.risk: Follow gym filming and privacy rules; family consent for minors.

items.name: Best and Worst Holds
items.setup: A list of hold types: directionals (undercling, sidepull, gaston), crimp, pinch, sloper.
steps: Each kid chooses a favorite and least favorite.
Share out loud if time allows.
Climb at least one route or 2–3 boulders featuring each.
items.why: Kids name and practise weaknesses, not just strengths.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: pictures of holds.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Marked Routes
items.setup: Bright paper tags on the route cards of climbs chosen for the class.
steps: Kids climb only tagged routes that day.
Remove all tags after class.
items.why: Steers kids onto chosen hold or wall types and keeps them in the right area.
items.variations: Tag by theme: all slopers this week.
items.risk: Tags keep kids on climbs coaches have checked.

items.name: I Went to the Wall…
items.setup: A bouldering wall with varied holds.
steps: The coach says “I went to the wall and found a…” plus 1–4 hold types.
Everyone finds and uses those holds properly.
Move around between calls.
items.why: Builds hold recognition and correct use.
items.variations: Mini progression: one hold type at a time for younger kids.
items.risk: Spread climbers across the wall.

items.name: Find That Hold
items.setup: One rope as a guide line and one container with one of every hold type. Blindfolds optional.
steps: One person at a time is blindfolded, or closes their eyes.
Call a hold type. They crawl along the rope, feel for it, and bring it back.
The group is done when every hold type has been found.
items.why: Teaches hold types by touch, with one shared goal for the class.
items.variations: No blindfold for younger kids: eyes closed.
items.risk: Crawl only; clear floor.

items.name: Blindfolded Hold ID
items.setup: A bucket of holds; a blindfold.
steps: A blindfolded kid picks a hold from the bucket (or is led to the wall).
Feel it and name the type.
Switch.
items.why: Climbing is tactile; knowing holds by feel is the first step to using them.
items.variations: Rock Game: get to know a rock, pass them behind backs and find yours by touch.
items.risk: Belay-line game: stay out of the belayer's space.

items.name: Wall Types
items.setup: Groups of 2 or 3; a sheet of wall types.
steps: Each kid climbs one route on every wall type (slab, vertical, overhang, arete, corner).
The class checks off a wall type when someone has climbed it.
items.why: Kids feel how wall angle changes technique.
items.variations: Edit the sheet to fit ability.
items.risk: Roped walls with a checked belayer.
coachingCues: Slab: less than vertical, often about balance, footwork, and smearing.
Vertical: essentially perpendicular to the floor.
Overhang: steeper than vertical; expect more need for body tension and straight arms.
commonMistakes: Treating every wall the same and only pulling with the arms, especially on slab.

progressions.easier: Compare two easy problems on two angles.
progressions.harder: The same movement cue (quiet feet or straight arms) on slab and on an overhang.

equipment: Access to more than one wall angle

items.name: Learn the Grades
items.setup: A stack of route cards.
steps: The group puts the cards in order from easiest to hardest.
They work together until the order is right.
items.why: Kids learn how the YDS and V scales work.
items.variations: Pair new climbers with experienced ones.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: ABCs of Climbing
items.setup: Groups of 3–6; one A–Z worksheet and a pencil each.
steps: Set an 8–10 minute timer.
Fill in a climbing word for each letter.
See how many you can fill, then try to beat your own list next time.
items.why: Fast vocabulary review.
items.variations: Ages 4–6 and Ages 6–9: coach writes, kids say.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Traffic Jam
items.setup: A tarp with a grid; a coach knows a secret path.
steps: Players line up beside the grid and step in one at a time, silently.
Paths go sideways or forward only.
A wrong square gets “Traffic Jam!” and the team starts over.
items.why: Teamwork and memory without talking.
items.variations: Shorter paths for younger kids.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Belly Breathing
items.setup: Seated, then on an easy wall.
steps: Sit, close eyes, breathe so the belly grows and shrinks.
Then on the wall: a belly breath each move while sinking the weight lower.
Talk about how it felt.
items.why: Calm breathing relaxes the grip and helps with nerves.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): balloon belly. Ages 12+ (training): count 4 in, 4 out at rests. Ages 14+: compare breathing on onsight and redpoint grades.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Pace Yourself
items.setup: Different routes; a belayer with a timer.
steps: Climb at slower and faster paces on different terrain.
Time each and notice what feels natural.
items.why: Steep or hard climbs need you to move faster through cruxes.
items.variations: Pair with Fartlek.
items.risk: Stop when form breaks.

items.name: Tennis Ball Focus
items.setup: 1–2 tennis balls per climber; open wall space.
steps: On the wall, throw a ball against the wall and catch it one-handed.
Progress to two balls, overhand and underhand.
items.why: Hand-eye coordination and balance while focused on something else.
items.variations: If catching is hard, bounce it off the ground instead.
items.risk: Low holds; nobody behind the thrower.

items.name: Pre-Climb Routine
items.setup: Any climb.
steps: Check (partner check or fall zone).
Breathe twice.
Read the first moves.
Say a cue word, then go.
items.why: A repeatable routine lowers nerves and builds consistency, especially at comps.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: three steps. Ages 14+: individual routines.
items.risk: The check comes first, every time.

items.name: Goal Setting & Training Log
items.setup: Notebooks or a shared log.
steps: Write one goal at the start of the month.
Each session, log what you climbed and one thing you learned.
Review monthly.
items.why: Tracking effort and learning supports a mastery mindset.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: sticker chart. Ages 14+: training block notes.
items.risk: Log pain or soreness too, and tell a coach.

items.name: Smooth Repeat
items.setup: A climb the climber has already sent.
steps: Climb it again more smoothly: fewer readjustments, quieter feet.
Rate smoothness 1–5 and try to improve.
items.why: Repeating a known climb lets kids focus on quality.
items.variations: Partner rates smoothness.
items.risk: Easy terrain.
coachingCues: Repeat an easy climb with the aim of looking smoother, not faster or harder.
Gresham's warm-up loop is a useful cue list: precise feet, straight arms, relaxed grip, fluid moves.
commonMistakes: Raising the grade on the repeat, which usually brings back rushed, bent-arm movement.

progressions.easier: One quality repeat of a climb they already know.
progressions.harder: Two or three repeats, adding one cue at a time (feet, then arms).

equipment: An easy known boulder or top-rope

items.name: Choose-Your-Level Ladder
items.setup: Three or four problems of rising difficulty for each climber.
steps: Climbers pick where to start.
Move up a rung after a send, down after two falls.
items.why: Lets each child work at the right challenge (mastery, not ranking).
items.variations: Celebrate personal bests.
items.risk: Fall zones clear between rungs.

items.name: Climbing Science
items.setup: Whiteboard or a demo on low holds.
steps: Explain one idea: friction, center of gravity, levers, or how a belay device adds friction.
Demonstrate it.
Climbers test it on the wall.
items.why: Understanding why a technique works helps older kids use it.
items.variations: Pick a weekly topic.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: Teach-Back
items.setup: Pairs or small groups.
steps: One climber teaches a skill to another (with a coach listening).
Swap.
items.why: Teaching is the best test of understanding.
items.variations: Ages 14+ teaches a skill to a younger group with a coach present.
items.risk: Coaches verify anything involving ropes or systems.

items.name: Team Send Board
items.setup: A whiteboard tally.
steps: Set a group goal (total sends or vertical feet).
Each send goes on the board.
Celebrate when the group hits it.
items.why: A shared goal builds team culture and volume.
items.variations: Monthly team goals.
items.risk: Quality over quantity; stop when form breaks.

items.name: Precision Speed
items.setup: An easy, known route.
steps: Climb it fast but with perfect foot placements.
Any readjustment means slow down next lap.
items.why: Keeps precision when moving quickly.
items.variations: Partner calls readjustments.
items.risk: Easy terrain.

items.name: Redpoint Tactics
items.setup: A project route.
steps: Break it into sections.
Work moves, then link sections.
Plan rests and clips; go for the redpoint.
items.why: Teaches the process of working a hard climb.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training) on boulders.
items.risk: Rest between attempts; watch fingers.

items.name: Limit Bouldering
items.setup: Hard boulders near the climber's max; long rests.
steps: Few attempts per problem.
Rest 3–5 minutes between tries.
Stop when quality drops.
items.why: Short, high-quality efforts build power.
items.variations: Pair with Limit Add-On (see Add-On).
items.risk: Older teens only; limit volume; watch fingers and shoulders.
coachingCues: This is for Ages 14+ only: a few high-quality tries on problems near the climber’s max, with 3–5 minutes of rest between attempts.
Stop when quality drops — more tired tries are not better practice.
commonMistakes: Too many attempts, or resting too little, so the session turns into exhausted repeats.
Ignoring finger or shoulder discomfort and ‘one more try’ after quality has already dropped.
Choosing problems with very small edges, shallow pockets or monos, which the book flags as poor value for the finger risk.

progressions.easier: Limit add-on on slightly sub-max moves with the same long rests.
progressions.harder: True limit tries only while movement quality stays high, then stop.

equipment: Hard boulders near the climber’s max

items.name: 4x4s
items.setup: Four boulders well within ability (ideally ones you've done).
steps: Climb each problem 4 times in a row with little rest.
After all four, traverse very easily for about 4 minutes instead of sitting down.
Repeat for 4 sets.
items.why: Classic power-endurance circuit. Keep the problems below max and stop each set before a total pump: easy traversing between sets helps the next effort more than sitting on the mats.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): 3x3 or easier problems.
items.risk: Problems well below max; stop if form breaks down or the forearms reach a full pump. Consider Crux-and-Traverse Intervals as the main version.

items.name: Two in a Row
items.setup: An onsight-grade route; belay pairs.
steps: Climb, lower, climb again with little rest.
Switch with your belay partner.
items.why: More climbing time and endurance.
items.variations: Downclimb instead of lowering.
items.risk: Partner check each time you re-tie or re-clip.

items.name: Climb Your Age
items.setup: Pairs of similar age; the whole class period.
steps: Each climbs as many pitches as they are years old.
Downclimbing can count as a pitch; 2x2s help.
Rules: no repeats, mixed styles.
items.why: Endurance and energy management over many climbs.
items.variations: Older kids: half their age.
items.risk: Rest between pitches whenever you need it; belay checks every climb.

items.name: Climbing Pyramid
items.setup: A pyramid template for each kid.
steps: Onsight grades on the bottom, project at the top, one grade in between.
Climb six climbs: start bottom left, go up, then down the right side.
items.why: Structured volume and a clear plan.
items.variations: Bigger pyramid for Ages 14+.
items.risk: End on easy climbs.
coachingCues: Build the pyramid before climbing: onsight grades at the bottom, a project at the top, and one grade in between.
Climb six problems: start bottom left, go up, then down the right side, and end on easier climbs.
commonMistakes: Starting at the project or stacking too many hard tries so quality drops before the easy finish.
Treating the pyramid as a contest against someone else’s grades instead of a personal volume plan.

progressions.easier: A smaller pyramid of known, moderate problems with longer rests.
progressions.harder: A bigger pyramid for Ages 14+, still ending on easy climbs.

equipment: A written pyramid template for each climber

items.name: Easy Continuous Laps
items.setup: An easy traverse, or an auto belay with staff permission.
steps: Climb easy terrain continuously for several minutes.
Keep the pump at about 1–2 on a 1–5 scale; if it climbs higher, slow down or use bigger holds.
items.why: Low-intensity volume with a light grip keeps blood flowing through the forearms, which builds the capillaries behind endurance.
items.variations: Ages 12+ (training): 3–5 minutes. Ages 14+: longer.
items.risk: Very easy terrain only.

items.name: Power Endurance Circuits
items.setup: A circuit of moderate moves (20–30).
steps: Climb the circuit, rest equal time, repeat.
items.why: Trains climbers to keep moving well under a manageable pump, like a sustained route, without letting it reach a full pump.
items.variations: Fewer moves for Ages 12+ (training).
items.risk: Older teens only; stop when form breaks.

items.name: Harness Check
items.setup: Harnesses laid out on the mat.
steps: Step in: leg loops not twisted, waist above the hips, buckles doubled back or locked.
Freeze for a coach check and name each part you checked.
Accuracy is the goal. Try again until the check is complete.
items.why: Makes the harness routine automatic. A complete check matters more than speed.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: coach helps, kid names each part. Ages 12+ (training): check a partner's harness too.
items.risk: A coach checks every harness before anyone leaves the ground.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (if using for auto belay)
coachingCues: Waist belt at the waist (not the hips), leg loops snug, buckle doubled back if the harness uses that design, belay loop free and visible.
Tie-in points are the two bridges beside the belay loop; the belay loop is for the belay device or an auto-belay connector, not for the tie-in knot on a standard sit harness.
Always check the knot, and check a locking carabiner is closed, locked, and loaded on the major axis.
commonMistakes: A waist belt worn too low, or a buckle that is not secured in the way that harness requires.
Confusing gear loops (for racking only) with the belay loop or tie-in points.

progressions.easier: Coach and climber point through a printed or on-harness checklist.
progressions.harder: Partners find one planted error (twisted leg loop or unlocked locker) and fix it.

equipment: Optional locker and device for the belay-loop check

items.name: Partner Check
items.setup: Belay pairs, tied in and ready.
steps: Check each other: harness buckles, figure-8 finished and through both tie-in points, belay device and locked carabiner on the belay loop, rope end knotted.
Say it out loud and point at each item.
items.why: A spoken, pointed check is the habit that catches mistakes.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: coach-led check song. Ages 14+: lead-specific additions.
items.risk: No check, no climb, every time.
coachingCues: Check each other every time: harness (waist and legs), knot, device, and locking carabiner.
On a standard sit harness, the rope goes through both tie-in points, not through the belay loop.
Petzl's harness notice: “Tie in to the two tie-in points. Always check the knot before starting to climb.”
commonMistakes: Clipping or tying in through the belay loop, or through only one tie-in point.
A locker that is not closed and locked, or is loaded off its major axis.

progressions.easier: Coach talks through each point while partners point at it.
progressions.harder: Partners run the check from memory, coach listens in and only prompts if a step is skipped.

items.name: Knot Practice
items.setup: Spare ropes on the belay line.
steps: Teach or review a knot.
Kids help teach each other.
Each climber ties it until it is complete and dressed, then checks a partner's knot.
items.why: Keeps waiting climbers engaged while building an essential roped-climbing skill.
items.variations: Teach new knots to interested climbers.
items.risk: Practice knots never replace a coach check on a real tie-in.
coachingCues: Each climber ties the knot until it is complete and dressed, then checks a partner’s knot. A practice knot never replaces a coach check on a real tie-in.
Waiting climbers stay engaged by teaching a partner the same steps.
commonMistakes: Stopping at a loosely dressed knot, or skipping the partner check.
Climbing on a knot that only a peer has seen.

progressions.easier: Figure-8 follow-through only, with a coach-tied model in view.
progressions.harder: Add a stopper if the gym requires it, still finishing with a coach check before any climb.

items.name: Spot the Figure 8
items.setup: Pre-tied knots, some correct and some not (or photos).
steps: Kids sort correct and incorrect figure-8s.
Explain what's wrong in each.
items.why: Recognizing a correct knot is the first step to checking one.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: count the five pairs of strands.
items.risk: Practice ropes only.
coachingCues: Sort correct and incorrect figure-8 follow-throughs, and explain what is wrong in each incorrect one.
For Ages 6–9, count the five pairs of strands on every ‘correct’ knot.
commonMistakes: Calling a messy or short-tailed knot correct because it ‘looks like an 8.’
Using these practice ropes as a substitute for a coach check on a real tie-in.

progressions.easier: Photos or clearly contrasting coach-tied models.
progressions.harder: Finer errors (crossed strands, short tail, only one tie-in point) that still have to be named.

equipment: Pre-tied practice knots or photos, some correct and some not

items.name: Flake and Coil
items.setup: Spare rope sections.
steps: Show how to flake a rope and why, and how to coil it.
Each climber practises until the rope feeds without a tangle.
items.why: Rope handling for future lead and outdoor climbing.
items.variations: One climber practises while a partner watches the pile.
items.risk: Low risk.

items.name: What Is Wrong?
items.setup: A quiet top-rope wall; coaches set up with deliberate mistakes.
steps: Coaches prepare to climb with things done wrong: leg loops upside down, shoes too big, chalk bag like a purse, laces undone, device on the tie-in loop instead of the belay loop, decorative carabiners.
The class finds what's wrong and what risk each mistake creates.
items.why: Kids learn to spot problems before a climb starts.
items.variations: Kids set up mistakes for each other (coach-supervised).
items.risk: Mistakes are shown on the ground only; nobody climbs on them.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (when demo includes auto belay)
coachingCues: Set the mistakes on the ground only: upside-down leg loops, a device on a tie-in loop instead of the belay loop, unlocked locker, and similar visible errors.
The class names what is wrong and what risk each mistake creates. Nobody climbs on a wrong setup.
commonMistakes: Showing a wrong setup in a live belay or auto-belay lane (auto-belay demos still need staff permission, and they stay on the ground).
Stopping at ‘that looks odd’ without naming the specific problem (wrong clip-in point, unlocked gate, harness upside down).

progressions.easier: Coach-set mistakes, one at a time.
progressions.harder: Kids set mistakes for each other, still coach-supervised, still on the ground.

equipment: Harnesses, shoes, and a belay device on the ground
A quiet top-rope or teaching area, no live climbing on the demo

items.name: Climbing Commands Call-and-Response
items.setup: Group on the mat.
steps: Coach calls a command; kids answer: “On belay?” – “Belay on.” “Climbing.” – “Climb on.” “Take.” – “Got you.” “Lower.” – “Lowering.”
Mix up the order; whoever answers wrong leads the next round.
items.why: Clear, standard commands manage risk on every climb.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: “Ready?” – “Ready!” Ages 14+: add lead calls like “slack” and “clipping”.
items.risk: Always use the gym's standard commands.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
coachingCues: American start-up is a question and answer: “On belay?” / “Belay on.” Then “Climbing.” / “Climb on.”
The belayer does not take the climber off belay until the agreed end-of-climb commands are finished.
Commands happen after the partner check, not instead of it.
commonMistakes: The climber leaving the ground before hearing “Climb on.”
Mumbling commands so the partner cannot tell they were answered.

progressions.easier: Practice on the ground with a rope through a dummy anchor or held by a coach.
progressions.harder: Full start-up on a real top-rope after a complete partner check.

items.name: Ground School Belay
items.setup: A rope through a low anchor or a coach holding the climber end; a backup belayer.
steps: Practise the belay motion (pull, brake, under, slide) with a coach.
Hold the brake strand at all times.
Progress to a backed-up belay on the wall.
items.why: Builds the brake-hand habit before any real weight.
items.variations: Ages per gym policy; teens follow belay test steps.
items.risk: Backup belayer and coach supervision until certified.
coachingCues: Practise pull, brake, under, slide with a coach, holding the brake strand at all times, before any real climber weight.
Progress to a backed-up belay on the wall only after the motion is consistent on the ground.
commonMistakes: Letting the brake hand leave the brake strand while sliding back up the rope.
Moving to a real climber too soon, without a backup and coach supervision.

progressions.easier: A rope through a low anchor or a coach holding the climber end, no wall yet.
progressions.harder: A backed-up belay on the wall, still under coach eyes until the gym’s certification.

equipment: Rope through a low anchor or coach-held climber end

items.name: Astronaut Lowering
items.setup: A top-rope route.
steps: At the top, sit back like in a chair with feet flat on the wall.
Walk down like an astronaut while being lowered.
items.why: Teaches the lowering position and builds trust in the rope.
items.variations: Start from a low height for nervous kids.
items.risk: Belayer lowers slowly; feet stay out in front.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (auto-belay version)
coachingCues: At the top, sit back like in a chair with feet flat on the wall, then walk down like an astronaut while being lowered.
The belayer lowers slowly; feet stay out in front. Start from a low height for nervous kids.
An auto-belay version still needs staff permission, and young climbers stay staff-clipped.
commonMistakes: Letting go of the wall and spinning, or pulling in tight so the feet leave the wall.
A fast lower before the climber has sat and found the feet-on-the-wall position.

progressions.easier: Start from a low height on an easy top-rope route.
progressions.harder: From the top of a longer easy route, still with a slow lower and feet walking down.

equipment: Top-rope route (or auto belay with staff permission)

items.name: Top-Rope Fall Practice
items.setup: A top-rope route with an attentive belayer.
steps: Climb a little way, call “falling”, and let go.
Increase height and slack slowly.
Climber chooses when to progress.
items.why: Gradual exposure builds trust in the rope.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: “sit in the chair” version.
items.risk: Belayer keeps the rope snug; check the fall line is clear.

items.name: Lead Fall Progression
items.setup: Steep, clean terrain; a qualified lead belayer and coach.
steps: Start with falls at the clip, then slightly above.
Progress gradually as the climber chooses.
Practise falling posture: look at the wall, legs bent, arms off the rope.
items.why: Lead falls are a skill to practise with care, not avoid.
items.variations: Only after the climber is lead-certified.
items.risk: Steep, clear terrain; experienced lead belayer; coach present.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, after lead certification or in a clinic, on steep, clean terrain, with a qualified lead belayer and a coach.
Start with falls at the clip, then slightly above, and progress only as the climber chooses.

Practise falling posture: look at the wall, legs bent, arms off the rope. Being comfortable with falling helps climbers stay focused on the movement; keep practice gradual and approachable rather than starting with a big jump above the last clip.
commonMistakes: Starting with a long fall above the draw, or practising on a ledgey, less-steep line.
Grabbing the rope or the draw during the fall, or continuing after the climber no longer wants the next step.

progressions.easier: A short fall at the clip, climber chooses when.
progressions.harder: Slightly above the clip, still on steep, clean ground, still at the climber’s pace.

researchSources.title: A fresh look at fall practice

items.name: Ground Clipping Practice
items.setup: Quickdraws on a low bolt or board.
steps: Practise clipping with both hands.
Check rope direction to avoid back-clipping.
Avoid z-clipping by grabbing rope close to the knot.
items.why: Correct clipping is automatic before it's used up high.
items.variations: Timed clipping drills.
items.risk: On the ground only until certified.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, on the ground. Practise clipping with both hands, and check rope direction so the clip is not a back-clip.
Avoid Z-clipping by grabbing rope close to the knot. Stay on the ground until certified.
commonMistakes: Only practising the preferred hand, or not looking at which way the rope runs through the draw.
Moving this drill onto a live lead wall too soon.

progressions.easier: One draw on a board, slow clips with each hand.
progressions.harder: Several draws, then a personal accuracy set (count your own correct clips), not a race.

equipment: Quickdraws on a low bolt or board

images.alt: Quickdraws made of two carabiners and a sling, the equipment used for ground clipping practice.

items.name: Mock Lead
items.setup: Top rope plus a second rope trailing to clip.
steps: Climb on top rope while clipping a second rope into draws.
Coach checks clips.
items.why: Practises lead skills with a top-rope backup.
items.variations: Add timed clips.
items.risk: Top rope is the real belay; the lead rope is for practice only.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays (if auto-belay backup)
Top-rope backup or auto-belay backup checked
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only. Climb on top rope (or on an auto belay with staff permission) while clipping a second rope into draws. The backup is the real belay.
The coach checks clips for back-clips, Z-clips, and rope behind the leg.
commonMistakes: Treating the practice lead rope as if it would catch a fall.
Clipping in a hurry without a coach check of each draw.

progressions.easier: Pre-hung draws, unhurried clips, top-rope backup.
progressions.harder: More clips on a longer easy line, still with a checked backup; a timed clip is optional only after accuracy is consistent.

equipment: Top rope plus a second trailing rope

images.alt: Climber clipping a quickdraw on a lead wall — a model of the clipping movement practised on mock lead, for Ages 12+ and 14+ with a real backup belay.

items.name: Spotting Practice
items.setup: A low boulder.
steps: Spotter stands with soft hands near the climber's hips.
Guide the fall toward the mat; don't catch.
items.why: Spotting directs falls to manage risk on boulders.
items.variations: Parent & Child (ages 2–3): parent spotting hands.
items.risk: Spot only low problems.
coachingCues: The spotter stands ready with soft hands near the climber’s hips, and guides the fall toward the mat rather than trying to catch the climber.
Spot only low problems, with a clear mat, and talk through the landing before the climb.
commonMistakes: Hands down, looking away, or standing too far from the likely landing.
Trying to grab the climber around the chest or arms, or spotting a high problem.

progressions.easier: Parent or coach spotting on a very low problem, with the child feeling a guided step-down.
progressions.harder: Peer spotting on low problems under coach eyes, still guiding to the mat, not catching.

images.alt: Spotter standing behind a low boulder with hands up near the climber’s hips, crash pads on the ground, ready to guide a fall toward the mat.

items.name: Fall Zones Tour
items.setup: Walk the gym.
steps: Point out fall zones under each wall.
Practise walking around, not under, climbers.
Teach three golden rules: look up, stay off mats under climbers, listen to coaches.
items.why: Kids learn where risk is in the gym.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: ‘wiggle zone’ and ‘fall zone’.
items.risk: Ongoing coach supervision.
coachingCues: The fall zone is the area under and around a climber where they might land; it stays clear of people, bags, and gaps between pads.
Walk the gym and point to good closed-pad areas and to places that are not landing zones.
Auto belays, if you visit them, are staff-permission only; the connector clips to the belay loop, not to multiple hard points.
commonMistakes: Standing on a pad to chat or film while someone is climbing above it.
Clipping an auto belay without staff permission, or clipping anything other than the belay loop.

progressions.easier: A walking tour with the group pointing out zones.
progressions.harder: Students lead a short tour for a partner and correct one staged mistake (a bag on a pad).

equipment: The gym floor and pads; no extra gear

items.name: Pass the Animal
items.setup: A soft toy, and a shelf, bucket or big jug as a hand-off spot at the edge of each wall panel; one climber per panel on a low traverse.
steps: The first climber carries the toy across their panel and leaves it on the hand-off spot.
They step down; then the next climber climbs to the spot, picks up the toy and carries it across their own panel.
Count the team's hand-offs in one round and try to beat that count next round.
items.why: Climbing one-handed while carrying the toy teaches balance, and the team count motivates without ranking.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: pass while on top rope next to each other.
items.risk: One climber per panel, and nobody climbs toward, above or below another climber.

items.name: Beat Your Own Time
items.setup: 1–2 problems or a short list of routes well below each climber's max flash grade; a stopwatch per climber or pair.
steps: Each climber picks their climbs and an order; one climber on a climb at a time.
Time your own lap from first touch to a controlled finish, topping or downclimbing.
Rest, then try to beat your own time while keeping feet quiet and placements clean.
Write your best in your log. Times are never compared between climbers.
items.why: Smooth, efficient movement under a clock, measured only against your own best. Planning your own list also builds pacing.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one easy boulder and two tries. Ages 12+ (training): a short circuit of 3–4 routes. Ages 14+: count your own clean laps in 5 minutes and beat last week's count.
items.risk: The next climber starts only after the last has landed and cleared the mat; moving on never skips partner checks; stop if form breaks down.

items.name: Welcome to the Wall
items.setup: Floor spots or tape marks on the mat about 8 inches from a low traverse; 3–4 spots per panel.
steps: Kids line up at one end of the wall.
Everyone walks slowly along the wall in one direction, hands on handholds and feet only on the floor spots.
Feel the holds and pick the ones you'd use if you were climbing; keep an arm's length apart.
After two or three passes, talk about which holds felt best and why.
items.why: Everlast uses it as a first-day, no-climbing introduction: kids touch holds and practise hand-foot coordination with zero height, which lowers first-day nerves.
items.variations: Parent & Child 2–3: walk it holding the parent's hand. Ages 3–4: name each hold's color as you touch it. Ages 6–9: on the last pass, lift one foot onto the lowest foothold for a breath.
items.risk: One direction of travel only, arm's length spacing, and nobody walks under another climber's fall zone.
coachingCues: Name the three wall angles: a slab leans away, vertical is essentially perpendicular to the floor, an overhang leans toward the climber.
Walk the group to one example of each in this gym before they climb.
commonMistakes: Sending everyone to the steepest wall first because it looks exciting.

progressions.easier: Touch a slab, a vertical wall, and an overhang from the ground.
progressions.harder: Climb a short easy problem on two different angles and say what the feet had to do.

equipment: Access to slab, vertical, and overhanging walls

items.name: Target Practice
items.setup: Beanbags or soft objects placed on holds along a low traverse; hoops or tape shapes on the mat as targets.
steps: One climber per panel; the next starts when the one ahead reaches the second panel.
On each panel, take one object off a hold and toss it into a target on the floor.
Reach the end, climb down, step off the mats and rejoin the line.
Count the group's total hits and try to beat it next round.
items.why: Letting go with one hand to throw trains one-handed balance and weight over the feet; a group total keeps it about personal and team bests.
items.variations: Ages 3–4: big targets right below the wall. Ages 6–9: objects on very high or very low holds. Ages 9–12: targets farther away or smaller. Seasonal themes: pumpkins into harvest hoops, or bean bags into jack-o'-lantern targets.
items.risk: Use only soft targets on the mats (hoops, tape), never hard buckets under the fall line; throwers wait until the mat in front is clear.
coachingCues: The target is reached with the same footwork as any other climb; looking at the target does not mean skipping feet.
One climber in the fall zone at a time.
commonMistakes: Jumping for the target from too far away when a static reach would work.

progressions.easier: A large, low target.
progressions.harder: A slightly higher target the climber can still touch with control and climb down from.

equipment: A visible target (tape, magnet, or marker)

items.name: Catch-n-Climb
items.setup: One soft ball per wall panel; a tosser standing at the edge of the mat in front of each panel; a tally sheet.
steps: Climbers traverse with one climber per panel and a steady line waiting.
When a climber is level with a tosser, they stop, turn, catch the ball one-handed and toss it back.
Climbers and tossers count successful catches and add them to the group sheet.
Swap tossers and climbers so everyone does both.
items.why: Catching while on the wall forces a stable stance and good weight on the feet; Everlast frames it as a whole-group goal of most total catches.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: underhand tosses from close. Ages 9–12: different ball sizes. Ages 12+: set a group catch target before starting and try to beat it.
items.risk: Soft balls only; tossers stay at the edge of the mats, never under a climber; keep one climber per panel.

items.name: Spell It Out
items.setup: Letter cards placed on holds along a traverse.
steps: Give the group a word.
One at a time, each climber traverses and collects the next letter in the word; one letter per climber.
Climbers on the floor help find where the next letter is.
Lay the letters out in order on the floor until the word is spelled.
items.why: Every climber's turn moves the team toward one shared result, and searching for a letter makes kids scan and move across the whole wall.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: their own name or a three-letter word. Ages 6–9: climbing words (SMEAR, CRIMP). Ages 9–12: letters on harder holds or higher.
items.risk: One climber on the traverse at a time per section; the spotting line stays outside the fall zone.

items.name: Number Pairs
items.setup: Cards numbered 1–10 placed on holds along a traverse.
steps: Pair climbers up and give each pair a target total (for example 9).
Each partner traverses and collects one card so the pair's two cards add up to the target.
Pairs plan which numbers to fetch before getting on the wall.
Return the cards and give the next pair a new total.
items.why: Partners have to plan and communicate before climbing, and the collected cards give a clear finish without ranking anyone.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: totals under 10. Ages 9–12: subtraction or multiplication, bigger numbers, or three cards per pair.
items.risk: One climber per section; partners wait off the mats.

items.name: Beta Map
items.setup: Part 1: a 4x4 grid of loose holds or spots on the floor. Part 2: a spray wall or traverse area. The coach secretly maps a start-to-finish sequence.
steps: The first climber stands on the start and moves to any neighboring spot; the coach says yes or no.
A right move means go again; a wrong move ends the turn and the next climber starts from the start, repeating the revealed sequence before guessing the next move.
Keep going until the whole sequence is found and every climber can move through it.
Repeat the same rules on the wall with a sequence every climber can do, starting with open feet.
items.why: Climbing Wall Association example game for planning, remembering and executing beta; the whole team succeeds together when the sequence is solved.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: floor version only, short sequence. Ages 9–12: on the wall with open feet. Ages 12+: feet on or off in the sequence.
items.risk: Wall sequence well below everyone's limit and low; waiting climbers stand off the mats.

items.name: Same Hand, Same Foot
items.setup: A vertical wall with lots of jugs.
steps: Place the right foot, then move the right hand.
Place the left foot, then move the left hand.
Keep arms long while moving the feet and shifting weight; bend them only to move up.
items.why: Momentum calls it the most basic movement pattern in climbing and recommends teaching it in a climber's first days, before route reading or flagging.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: say it out loud as they climb. Ages 9–12: add open and closed hip positions. Ages 12+: point out the exceptions (back flag, pogo).
items.risk: Easy, low terrain; stop and reset if arms bend and the climber locks up.
coachingCues: If the climber is reaching with the right hand, they should be driving, pulling, or pushing with the right foot — and the same on the left.
Keep the arms long while moving the feet and shifting weight; bend the arms only to move up.
This is the basic movement pattern to teach in a climber’s first days, before sequence reading.
commonMistakes: Thinking of hands and feet as separate jobs, so the opposite foot drives the reach.
Bending both arms and locking up instead of shifting weight with straight arms.

progressions.easier: Say ‘right foot, right hand’ out loud on a vertical jug wall.
progressions.harder: Point out the exceptions (a back flag, and the rarer pogo) once the basic pattern is solid.

equipment: Vertical wall with lots of jugs

items.name: Hip Rotation Drill
items.setup: An easy boulder.
steps: Climb it once turning the opposite hip to the wall (reach left hand, right hip in).
Climb it again turning the same-side hip to the wall (reach left hand, left hip in).
Talk about which felt more balanced and how much farther you could reach.
items.why: PitchSix uses the awkward first lap to make the same-side hip rotation rule obvious: better balance, less grip effort and more reach.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: big holds and a partner who calls which hip. Ages 12+: on steeper terrain. Ages 14+: combine with flagging.
items.risk: Well below limit; downclimb or step off when a position feels awkward.

items.name: Slow-Motion Climbing
items.setup: 6–8 boulders 2–3 grades below flash, including some the climber usually rushes.
steps: Climb each boulder as slowly and smoothly as possible: no jumping or swinging.
Set feet and hips before every reach; the move is continuous, not stop-start.
Rest a minute or two between boulders.
Move up a grade only when all of them stay slow and clean.
items.why: Blok Sessions: taking momentum away shows every sloppy foot placement and builds body tension and control.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: vertical walls with good feet, or slow only the feet. Ages 12+: add steeper terrain. Ages 14+: same boulders, slower.
items.risk: Steep slow moves load shoulders and core; stay on vertical terrain if a shoulder is sore and stop when movement gets scrappy.

items.name: Antagonist Push Set
items.setup: Floor space; light resistance bands or very light weights for shoulder rotations.
steps: Two sets of push-up plus (push-ups that finish by pushing the shoulder blades apart).
Two sets of dips (assisted if needed).
One set each of band external rotations and band face pulls or pull-aparts; no internal-rotation work.
Use loads light enough for about 20 reps; 15–20 minutes, two or three times a week.
items.why: Climbing trains pulling muscles; Eric Hörst and UKC's junior injury interviews recommend balancing them with push and rotator-cuff work to lower elbow and shoulder injury risk. The Science of Climbing Training adds that the lats and chest both rotate the arm inward, so balance comes from the upper-back muscles and the outward rotators, not from extra chest or inward-rotation work.
items.variations: Ages 12+: push-ups and band rotations only. Ages 14+: full set; add reverse wrist curls.
items.risk: Light loads and clean reps only; nothing to failure; no finger loading added.

items.name: Plumb Line
items.setup: A low traverse on a vertical wall. Tie a figure 8 (or a small carabiner) on a short cord and hang it from the climber's waist so it swings freely in front of the hips.
steps: Start the traverse with the line hanging in front of the hips.
A foot may only move when the plumb line hangs directly over the other foot.
Pause, shift the hips until the line settles over the standing foot, then move the free foot.
Traverse back the other way.
items.why: The line makes center of gravity visible: climbers see whether their weight is really over the standing foot before the next foot moves, which is the heart of weight transfer.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a beanbag on a string and a 'hips over the foot!' call. Ages 9–12: hands may only move while the line is still. Ages 12+: try a slightly steeper wall and notice how the hips have to come in.
items.risk: Keep the cord short so it cannot loop around a foot or a hold; low traverse only, never on a rope route.

items.name: Circle Circle
items.setup: A circle about 1–1.5 m across marked with chalk or tape on a low wall section with plenty of holds (or a hoop fixed flat to the wall).
steps: The climber starts on the wall at the edge of the circle.
For one minute, climb around the circle and count complete laps.
Rest, then try to beat your own lap count.
Switch direction each round.
items.why: Going round a circle mixes up, down and sideways moves without stepping off, so climbers practice changing direction, crossing and matching; counting your own laps is a personal-best goal.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: a big circle, any holds, count out loud together. Ages 6–9: climb inside the circle only. Ages 9–12: hands outside the circle, feet inside.
items.risk: A hoop must not be able to catch a foot (chalk or tape avoids that). Keep the circle low so every lap stays within jump-down height over mats.

items.name: Hidden Rest
items.setup: A traverse or easy route with a few spots where a one-hand or no-hands rest is possible (a big foot ledge, a corner, a volume).
steps: Demonstrate a few rest positions: weight over a big foothold, stemming in a corner, hips against a volume.
Climbers search the section for 'hidden rests' and show one to the group.
At each rest they let one hand hang loose for a few seconds, then swap, breathing slowly (both hands off only if the stance allows).
Climb the section again, using every rest they found.
items.why: Finding a stable position over a good base of support takes weight off the arms; climbers who spot rests climb longer before getting pumped.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: 'can you find a spot where you can wave both hands?' Ages 9–12: rate each rest good, okay or poor. Ages 12+ and 14+: plan rests from the ground, then check the plan on the route.
items.risk: Demonstrate first and give precise instructions; no-hands rests only low on the boulder wall or on top rope.
coachingCues: Show a few rest options first: weight over a big foothold, a stem in a corner, or hips against a volume.
At each rest, let one hand hang loose for a few seconds, then swap, breathing slowly; take both hands off only if the stance allows it.
Climb the section again using every rest the group found.
commonMistakes: Skipping rests and climbing straight through until the arms pump.
Trying a no-hands rest high on a boulder without a plan to step down.

progressions.easier: ‘Can you find a spot where you can wave both hands?’ on a low wall or top rope.
progressions.harder: Plan rests from the ground, then check the plan on the route.

equipment: Easy traverse or route with at least one stem, ledge, or volume rest

items.name: The Artist
items.setup: A sheet of paper with an outline of a face fixed to the wall at a reachable height, and a marker.
steps: Each climber climbs to the picture and adds one feature (an eye, a nose, a hat).
They draw with one hand while holding on with the other and both feet on holds.
Climb down; the next climber adds the next feature.
Finish the picture as a team and show it off.
items.why: Drawing frees one hand, so climbers must find a stable base of support first; the shared picture keeps everyone involved without ranking anyone.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: picture low, on big holds. Ages 6–9: reach the picture by a given route. Ages 9–12: the group names the next feature before each climber starts.
items.risk: Keep the picture within jump-down height on the bouldering wall and spot one-handed attempts; cap the marker between turns.

items.name: Posing
items.setup: A slab or vertical wall with lots of holds; the group sits on the mat.
steps: One climber gets on the wall and finds a funny or spectacular position (a star, a flag, a frog).
They hold it for three seconds while the group claps or cheers.
The group gives the pose a name.
The next climber tries a pose nobody has done yet.
items.why: Kids discover positions they would never try on a route, building coordination, body awareness and flexibility; the cheer celebrates creativity, not a ranking.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: coach names a shape (a star, a flag, a frog). Ages 9–12: each pose must use a named technique (drop knee, flag). Ages 12+: link three poses into a short sequence.
items.risk: Start new climbers on a slab before vertical; keep poses low and step down from awkward positions instead of letting go.
coachingCues: The pose is held for about three seconds while the group cheers the idea, not a ranking.
Invite a funny or spectacular shape — a star, a flag, a frog — and let the group name it.
The next climber tries a pose nobody has done yet.
commonMistakes: Turning the activity into a contest for the ‘best’ or highest pose.
Holding an awkward pose high on the wall and letting go instead of stepping down.

progressions.easier: Coach calls an animal theme on a low slab.
progressions.harder: Each pose must use a named technique, or link three poses into a short sequence.

equipment: Slab or vertical wall with lots of holds
Group sitting on the mat out of the fall zone

items.name: Rope Corridor
items.setup: Two ropes or cords stretched horizontally along a traverse, about knee height and shoulder height, forming a corridor.
steps: Traverse with both hands and both feet inside the corridor.
If a hand or foot lands outside, pause and fix it before moving on.
Traverse back.
items.why: A narrow band of usable holds forces small, precise moves and creative footwork.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a wide corridor. Ages 9–12: narrow it. Ages 12+: hands above the top rope line, feet inside the corridor.
items.risk: Fix the cords flat to the wall so nothing can snag a foot or finger; low traverse only.

items.name: Split the Line
items.setup: A rope or tape line running from bottom to top of a low wall section.
steps: Climb up with both hands on one side of the line and both feet on the other.
Climb down, then switch sides and go again.
items.why: Splitting hands and feet across a line forces climbers to lean, twist and flag to stay in balance.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: big holds near the line. Ages 9–12: shift the line so one side has few holds. Ages 12+: on a steeper panel.
items.risk: Low terrain over mats; tape the line flat so nothing swings into the climber.

items.name: Climb to the Beat
items.setup: A speaker and a playlist mixing slow and fast songs; an easy traverse.
steps: Play a slow song: climbers move slowly and smoothly with the tempo.
Switch to a fast song: move faster while keeping feet quiet.
Change songs without warning; climbers match the new tempo.
items.why: Matching movement to tempo trains pace control and smooth flow, contrasting slow precise movement with quick light movement.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: one move per drumbeat, counted out loud. Ages 9–12: one move per bar. Ages 12+: slow tempo on easy sections, brisk tempo through the hard part.
items.risk: Low traverse with climbers spread apart; keep the volume low enough to hear the coach.

items.name: Hip Watch Traverse
items.setup: A quickdraw clipped to the harness or a bright sticker at the climber's hip; an easy traverse with big footholds.
steps: Traverse sideways while keeping your eyes on the marker at your hip.
Notice how the hip turns in and out as you move.
Traverse again normally, keeping that hip close to the wall.
items.why: Watching the hip makes climbers aware of hip position and turning, which drives reach and balance on traverses.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: a sticker on the hip. Ages 9–12: turn the hip to the wall on each reach. Ages 12+: pair it with the Hip Rotation Drill.
items.risk: Big footholds and low terrain only, because the climber is not looking at their feet.

items.name: Lemon Lime
items.setup: A boulder problem one or two grades below the climber's max flash grade.
steps: Lemon: from the start holds, make the first move, then reverse back to the start.
Without coming off, make the first two moves and reverse to the start.
Keep adding one move until you reach the finish hold.
Lime: from the top, downclimb one move and climb back up; keep adding moves until you are back at the start.
items.why: Repeating and reversing every move builds endurance, sequence memory and downclimbing control on a single problem.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: lemon only, on a short, easy problem. Ages 9–12: lemon only. Ages 12+: full lemon and lime. Ages 14+: closer to flash grade.
items.risk: Choose problems well below max; stop when form breaks or fingers tire, and downclimb rather than fall from the top.

items.name: Special Number Climb
items.setup: Number cards taped high and low across a traverse wall, some that fit today's category and some that don't.
steps: Announce today's special number category (even, multiples of 5, prime).
Climbers spread out, one per wall panel.
On each panel, touch one card that fits the category and say it out loud.
Repeat the traverse finding different numbers.
items.why: Hunting for the right card makes climbers look around, reach and plan their path, with a classroom link and no ranking.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: even or odd. Ages 9–12: keep a running total of the numbers touched.
items.risk: One climber per panel; keep cards within the matted traverse height.

items.name: Hover Feet
items.setup: An easy traverse or boulder well below the climber's level.
steps: Lift a foot and hold it just above the next foothold for a slow count of two while watching it.
Place it on the best part of the hold and don't adjust it.
Repeat for every foot move; hands move as normal.
items.why: Hovering only works when the weight is balanced over the standing foot, and the pause makes the first placement exact; it builds the eye-to-foot habit.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: hover for a count of one. Ages 14+: steeper terrain or smaller footholds.
items.risk: Low traverse or top rope; step down if the standing leg starts to shake.
coachingCues: Look at the exact spot, hover the foot over it, then set it down. A hover followed by a shuffle does not count.
If the body swings during the hover, move the hips over the standing foot instead of pulling harder with the hands.
Every placement gets the hover, including easy ones near the ground.
commonMistakes: Picking boulders that are too hard, so the climber holds the hover with the arms.
Holding a swing with the hands instead of moving the hips over the standing foot.
Hovering without looking first.

progressions.easier: Longer hovers on easy, large footholds.
progressions.harder: The same hover on slightly harder boulders, then steeper walls or smaller footholds.

equipment: Easy boulder or traverse with clear footholds

researchSources.title: Hover feet for climbing: how to do it

items.name: Mantle Practice
items.setup: Low ledges, volume tops or boulder top-outs with thick mats underneath.
steps: Get both hands on top of the ledge.
Flip one hand palm-down and press, then bring a foot up, often right beside the hand.
Lean in over the feet and stand up. Do each mantle 3–5 times, both sides.
items.why: Mantles show up on most boulder top-outs, but kids rarely practise them on purpose; it's like climbing out of a pool.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: ‘climb out of the pool’ onto a stack of mats or a low volume. Ages 12+ (training): mantles with few or no footholds.
items.risk: Keep mantles low over thick mats; spot top-outs and keep the landing zone clear.
coachingCues: A mantle is how you climb through a ledge when there is nothing useful to pull on above it, like getting out of a pool.
Try a palm-down press, a hand-foot match, and leaning in over the feet.
It is commonly used when topping out a boulder.
commonMistakes: Keeping the hands as pulls above the lip instead of flipping them to a press.
Leaving the hips behind the ledge so the press has nothing under it.

progressions.easier: A low box, volume, or padded ledge they can press out onto.
progressions.harder: A higher top-out with a planned downclimb or drop after they stand up.

equipment: A ledge, volume, or top-out with pads underneath

images.alt: Climber topping out a boulder with a mantle: palms pressing down on the lip, body rising onto the shelf.

items.name: Drop-Knee Finder
items.setup: Easy overhanging boulders with big holds and footholds wide of the body.
steps: Try a move with the hips square to the wall.
Try it again, turning the knee on the same side as the reaching hand in and down while both big toes push on the footholds.
Compare the reach and arm effort. Find 4–6 moves where it helps and do each 3 times per side.
items.why: Feeling the with-and-without difference teaches when a drop knee takes weight off the arms.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: one or two big, obvious moves set by the coach. Ages 14+: smaller footholds and steeper walls.
items.risk: Drop knees load the knee: keep reps low, skip very deep or wide drop knees, and stop if the knee twinges.
coachingCues: Turn the knee on the same side as the reaching hand inward and down, with both big toes pushing on the footholds.
Compare the same move hips-square and with the drop knee so the climber feels the extra reach and lower arm effort.
Turn in, reach, then unwind — it is a position you pass through, not one to hang in.
commonMistakes: Rotating the wrong knee (it should be the knee on the same side as the reaching hand).
Pushing through the middle of the foot instead of the big toes, or forcing a very deep or wide drop knee on day one.

progressions.easier: Close footholds at about the same height, a shallow turn, and big handholds.
progressions.harder: Use the drop knee in the beta of harder steep problems once the easy versions feel automatic.

equipment: Easy overhanging boulders with big holds
items.duration: 20 min (Blok Sessions protocol: 5–6 moves, 3 tries per side)

images.alt: Climber on steep rock with one knee turned in and down, hip close to the wall, reaching past a high hold.

items.name: Barn-Door Fix
items.setup: A low move that makes the climber swing open (barn-door), such as a long reach off a sidepull.
steps: Try the move with an outside flag and notice where the body swings.
Try it again crossing the free leg behind the standing leg (back flag / reverse flag).
Talk through which version stopped the swing and why.
items.why: A back flag (also called a reverse flag) keeps balance through hand moves without moving the feet; comparing the two flags shows when to use it when X-motion is broken.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach sets one clear move. Ages 14+: climbers find barn-door moves on their own projects.
items.risk: Low problems over mats; an open swing can pull a climber off.

items.name: Place, Shift, Move
items.setup: A vertical or slab wall with tape on a few high footholds out to the side.
steps: Place: put a foot on a taped hold.
Shift: move the hips over that foot until the weight is fully on it.
Move: only then reach for the next hold, standing up with the leg rather than pulling. Do 3 slow tries per side.
items.why: The three-word cue makes the rock-over a repeatable sequence and shows that the legs do the lifting.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: say ‘place, shift, move’ out loud. Ages 12+ (training): higher footholds and smaller handholds.
items.risk: Low wall or top rope.
coachingCues: Use the three words in order: place the foot, shift the hips fully over it, then move the hand.
Stand up mainly with the leg; the arms are for balance, not for pulling through the rock-over.
Go slowly — get the hips genuinely over the foot before pushing.
commonMistakes: Reaching for the next hold before the weight has shifted, which makes the move much more physical or comes up short.
Placing the foot too low, or only practising the stronger side.

progressions.easier: Say ‘place, shift, move’ out loud on a vertical or slabby wall with a moderate foot height.
progressions.harder: Higher footholds and smaller handholds, three slow tries per side.

equipment: Tape to mark a few high footholds out to the side
items.duration: 23 min (Blok Sessions protocol: 3–5 moves, 3 slow tries per side)

items.name: Arch Circuit
items.setup: A wall section with two marked ends and a top height; tape or chalk.
steps: Climb up from one end, across at the top height and down the other end, like an arch.
Walk back to the start and climb another arch using different hand holds; tape each hold once it's used.
Count your rounds in a set time (1–5 minutes) and try to beat your own count next session.
items.why: Builds endurance and quick on-wall decisions, because the easy holds get used up.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: one minute and a low arch. Group version: the group shares one arch and sees how many different arches it can find together.
items.risk: One climber on an arch at a time; keep the arch low and the fall zone clear.

items.name: G-Tox Shake-Out
items.setup: A traverse or route with a good jug rest partway.
steps: At the rest, hang on a straight arm and shake the free arm down by your side.
Then alternate: hold the free arm above your head for a few seconds, then drop it below the waist.
Swap hands and notice which method helps you recover.
items.why: In a study reported by Training for Climbing, alternating the arm above the head and below the waist (G-Tox) recovered grip strength better than dangling alone. The Science of Climbing Training adds that shaking by itself has not been shown to help; what helps most is resting before a full pump, on a big hold, alternating hands and slowing the breath.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: learn to straight-arm and shake first. Ages 14+: use it on pumpy circuits.
items.risk: Practise on easy terrain; come down when pumped rather than hanging on.

items.name: Furthest-Point Traverse
items.setup: An easy traverse.
steps: Every new hand or foot placement must land further along than the last placement of any limb.
Plan which limb goes next; you'll need cross-throughs and step-throughs.
Traverse 8–12 moves, rest a minute, then go the other way. If you break the rule, go back one move.
items.why: Forces sequence planning, cross-throughs and hip turns.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: only the hands follow the rule. Ages 14+: longer traverses on steeper walls.
items.risk: Low traverse; rest between attempts.

items.name: One Thing at a Time
items.setup: Easy boulders.
steps: Move only one body part at a time: one hand, or one foot, or the hips.
Pause briefly after each movement.
Make it stricter: move the hips as their own step before each reach.
items.why: Shows where balance or sequence is off.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: robot voice and a ‘beep’ between moves. Ages 12+ (training): steeper terrain.
items.risk: Easy, low boulders.

items.name: Tendon Glides
items.setup: No equipment; seated or standing.
steps: Cycle smoothly through five hand shapes: fingers straight, tabletop, straight fist, hook fist, full fist.
Go for 45 seconds, rest 15 seconds; three rounds, both hands at once.
Follow with easy climbing.
items.why: Moves the finger tendons through their full range before they're loaded; it's a warm-up, not a strength exercise.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: name the shapes (flat, table, fist, hook, ball) as a follow-along.
items.risk: Gentle movement only; nothing should hurt.

items.name: Hollow Body Hold
items.setup: Mats.
steps: Lie on your back and press the lower back into the mat.
Lift the shoulders and legs a little off the mat, arms reaching past your head, and hold without the back arching.
Hold 10–15 seconds, 3–4 times with a minute's rest; make it harder (arms overhead, legs lower) rather than longer.
items.why: Bodyweight core tension that carries over to keeping the feet on steep walls; bodyweight exercises suit youth climbers.
items.variations: Easier: bend the knees or bring the arms to the sides, or do dead bugs (lower one arm and the opposite leg slowly while the back stays down).
items.risk: Quality over time; stop when the lower back lifts.

items.name: Comfort-Zone Ladder
items.setup: One move or boulder that feels a little scary but has a clean, well-padded landing: a high top-out, a committing slab move, a dyno.
steps: First try: go only as far as feels fine, then step or downclimb off.
Each next try: one small step further (one hold higher, one more move).
If a try feels more than a little scary, repeat the previous step. Finish on a step you'd gladly do again.
items.why: Small, chosen steps grow confidence without flooding the climber with fear.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach and climber agree the steps in advance. Ages 14+: pair with a written fear inventory after the session.
items.risk: Only over good landings, with spotting where useful; never practise above a poor landing.

items.name: Backstep Drill
items.setup: 5–6 easy, slightly overhanging boulders with footholds out to the side.
steps: On each reach, put the outside edge of the shoe on the same side as the reaching hand onto a foothold.
Turn that hip into the wall so the body goes sideways, then reach.
Climb each boulder 2–3 times, backstepping wherever it helps, and notice how much further you reach than with your chest square to the wall.
items.why: Blok Sessions calls turning the hip in the biggest reach gain available on steep walls; easy boulders keep the load low while the habit forms.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach marks the backstep footholds with tape. Ages 12+ (training): compare with Hip Rotation Drill. Ages 14+: move on to drop knees and twist locks, which build on the same hip turn.
items.risk: Keep it on easy, low boulders over good mats; a turned hip can swing open, so practise the move low before trying it higher.

items.name: Deadpoint Practice
items.setup: Easy boulders with 3–4 long reaches (skip holds to lengthen them).
steps: Choose an exact spot on the target hold, not just the hold.
Swing the hips toward it, push with the feet and catch that spot at the moment the body stops rising, with the feet staying on.
Do 5 tries per move with about a minute's rest, then climb 2–3 easy boulders using deadpoints wherever you can.
items.why: A deadpoint lengthens the reach while the feet stay on, so it replaces slow, strained lock-offs at a low cost.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: big target jugs at a short distance. Ages 12+ (training): smaller target holds. Ages 14+: deadpoints into sidepulls and on steeper walls.
items.risk: Catching a hold loads fingers and shoulders: use big targets, keep reps low and rest between tries; climbers coming back from a finger or shoulder injury should get cleared first.
coachingCues: Pick an exact spot on the target hold, not just the hold. Catch it at the moment the body stops rising, with the feet staying on.
Swing the hips toward the hold, push with the feet, and pull with the hands — five tries per move with about a minute of rest.
If the feet come off, that try was a dyno, not a deadpoint. Reset and keep pressure through the feet.
commonMistakes: Aiming at the hold instead of a spot on it, or catching early on the way up or late on the way down.
Cutting the feet, or rushing the rests so later tries become sloppy slaps.

progressions.easier: Big jugs, reaches the climber could almost make statically, on a vertical wall.
progressions.harder: Longer reaches, smaller targets, then deadpoints into sidepulls or on steeper walls.

equipment: Easy boulders or an easy circuit
items.duration: 21 min (Blok Sessions protocol: 3–4 moves, 5 tries each)
