items.name: Push-Off Fall Practice
items.setup: Slightly overhanging or clean vertical top-rope; experienced belayer; climber chooses height.
steps: Climb to a comfortable height on a snug top rope.
Bend the legs, push off the wall, relax the arms, and land back with soles of the feet, knees soft, feet about shoulder-width.
Repeat, pushing a little harder only while the climber still looks and sounds relaxed.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 1 builds falling skill inside the climber’s comfort zone before any lead falls; Prowess episode 1 similarly starts with controlled top-rope slumps the climber chooses.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: tiny push-offs only, coach belay. Ages 9–12: add a calm breath before each push. Ages 12+: progress later to sideways pendulum comfort, still on top rope.
items.risk: Belayer manages slack deliberately. Clear fall line. Climber decides when to stop. Prefer slightly overhanging terrain so the body swings into space, not into panels.
prereqs: Comfort sitting on the rope (Astronaut Lowering)

items.name: Pendulum Comfort on Top Rope
items.setup: Top rope with space to move sideways; belayer and coach agree the swing arc is clear of people and features.
steps: From a mid-height stance, walk or shuffle sideways on the wall until a gentle pendulum starts, then return.
When ready, add a small push at the end of the swing so the landing uses feet and bent knees.
Stop while it still feels manageable; talk about what the body did.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 2 specifically trains sideways falls and pendulum landings that real rope climbing produces when a climber is off the fall line.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: tiny side steps only with coach belay. Ages 14+: slightly larger swings on clean overhanging terrain.
items.risk: Coach-run only. Clear the entire swing arc. No King-Swing-sized offsets unless that separate activity is planned with full clearance.

items.name: Clip-and-Let-Go on Top Rope
items.setup: Top rope on a route with visible bolt hangers or draws beside the line; skilled belayer; climber already comfortable with push-off falls.
steps: Climb to a draw, touch it, and let go with minimal hesitation while arms stay relaxed.
Repeat at successive draws. Belayer starts snug and only adds a little slack when the climber asks and looks relaxed.
End on a fall the climber would gladly repeat.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 3 uses touch-and-let-go on top rope to read hesitation and body tension before any lead fall ladder.
items.variations: Keep it to two or three touches per session. If hesitation returns, drop back to Push-Off Fall Practice.
items.risk: Top rope only in this activity. Belayer skill matters. Slightly overhanging, clear terrain. Climber-led progression.

items.name: Progressive Top-Rope Slump
items.setup: Slightly overhanging top rope; climber brought to about the fourth bolt height and rested on the rope; belayer holds steady slack.
steps: From hanging on the rope, pull onto the wall and slump back without the belayer changing slack.
Pull on, make one move, and let go, returning near the same height.
Add moves only while the climber chooses; finish on a comfortable slump.
items.why: Prowess Climbing Coaching’s lead-fall episode 1 builds falling comfort on top rope with climber-chosen height before true lead falls.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: coach belay, fewer reps. Ages 12+: peer belay only if both are certified and a coach backs up.
items.risk: Fatigue raises stress—stop early if form or mood drops. Climber alone picks the biggest slump.

items.name: Take and Lower Sequence
items.setup: Top rope; belay pair; coach listening.
steps: At a rest or the top, climber calls “take” (or gym word); belayer takes rope tight and answers.
Climber sits, confirms weight on the rope, then calls “lower.”
Belayer lowers at a steady pace while climber keeps feet on the wall; finish with “off belay” / gym end calls only when standing on the ground.
items.why: Climb’s lead syllabus and every top-rope program treat clear take/lower communication as non-negotiable rope risk management.
items.variations: Ages 4–6: “ready / hold me / going down” simplified words matching the gym. Ages 9+: add “slack” and “that’s me” where the gym uses them.
items.risk: Always use the gym’s standard commands. Belayer’s brake hand never leaves the brake strand. Staff supervise uncertified belayers.
coachingCues: At a rest or the top, the climber calls ‘take’ (or the gym word); the belayer takes the rope tight and answers.
The climber sits, confirms weight is on the rope, then calls ‘lower.’ The belayer lowers at a steady pace while the climber keeps feet on the wall.
Finish with the gym’s end calls only when the climber is standing on the ground. The brake hand never leaves the brake strand.
commonMistakes: Lowering before the climber has sat and confirmed, or using words that are not the gym’s command set.
The brake hand coming off the brake strand, or a rushed lower with feet swinging off the wall.

progressions.easier: Simplified gym-matched words (‘ready / hold me / going down’) from a low height.
progressions.harder: Add ‘slack’ and ‘that’s me’ where the gym uses them, still with a staff-supervised uncertified belayer.

items.name: Belay Stance Practice
items.setup: Ground school rope through a low anchor or coach-held climber end; backup belayer; tube device or ABD per gym policy.
steps: Set an athletic stance, facing the wall, brake hand on the brake strand.
Practise taking in and paying out while keeping the stance; partner gives gentle body-weight tugs with a backup.
Name what changes for a heavier or lighter climber (stance, attention, possible ground anchor per gym rules).
items.why: Climb’s syllabus and GVSU lead lesson both list belayer positioning and weight-difference management as explicit learning objectives.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: stance and take-in only, coach as backup. Ages 12+: add soft-catch discussion for future lead belay, still ground-loaded.
items.risk: No live lead belaying until gym certification. Backup belayer required. Follow the gym’s device policy.
coachingCues: Set an athletic stance facing the wall, brake hand on the brake strand, and practise taking in and paying out while keeping that stance.
Name what changes for a heavier or lighter climber (stance, attention, and any ground anchor the gym uses).
No live lead belaying until gym certification. A backup belayer is required.
commonMistakes: A casual, narrow stance that gets pulled toward the wall on a tug.
The brake hand leaving the brake strand while the belayer adjusts their feet.

progressions.easier: Stance and take-in only, coach as backup, for Ages 9–12.
progressions.harder: Add a soft-catch discussion for future Ages 12+ or 14+ lead belay, still ground-loaded.

equipment: Ground-school rope through a low anchor or coach-held climber end

items.name: Figure-8 Dressing Lab
items.setup: Spare practice ropes; photos or coach-tied models of dressed and messy figure-8 follow-throughs.
steps: Tie a figure-8 follow-through through both tie-in points on a harness (practice harness on the ground).
Dress it: parallel strands, no big crosses, fist-length or gym-standard tail, optional stopper if the gym requires it.
Partner counts the five pairs of strands and traces the rope path before a coach confirms.
items.why: Climb’s day-1 tying block and Momentum knot practice both treat a correctly dressed figure-8 as the foundation of every partner check.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: finish one correct knot with heavy coach help; do not rush. Ages 9+: add spotting common errors (short tail, only one tie-in point, undressed twists).
items.risk: Practice knots never replace a coach check on a real tie-in. Nobody climbs on an unchecked knot.
coachingCues: Dress the knot so the strands sit parallel, with no big crosses, and leave a fist-length or gym-standard tail.
Have the partner count the five pairs of strands and trace the rope path through both tie-in points before a coach confirms.
If the gym requires a stopper, add it only after the figure-8 is dressed.
commonMistakes: Threading only one tie-in point, or clipping in instead of tying through both hard points.
Leaving a short tail or a messy, crossed knot and calling it done without a partner or coach check.

progressions.easier: Use a practice harness on the ground with a coach-tied model next to it.
progressions.harder: Time a calm dress-and-trace, still finishing with a coach check before any real climb.

items.name: Harness Parts Callout
items.setup: Harnesses on the mat; coach points, climbers name.
steps: Point to waist belt, leg loops, belay loop, tie-in points, gear loops, buckle.
Climbers repeat names, then swap: climber points, peer names.
End by showing the only clip-in point used for the auto-belay carabiner or belay device (belay loop) and the two tie-in points for the rope.
items.why: ABC auto-belay induction and Climb’s gear overview both start with harness attachment points because wrong clip-in points create serious loading problems.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 3–4: waist and leg loops only, with a parent. Ages 4–6: add belay loop. Ages 9+: add “why not clip both hard points” (tri-axial loading idea in kid words).
items.risk: Gear-loop carabiners are never load-bearing. Coach confirms every real clip-in.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
coachingCues: Name waist belt, leg loops, belay loop, tie-in points, gear loops, and buckle, then swap: climber points, peer names.
End by showing the only clip-in point used for an auto-belay carabiner or a belay device — the belay loop — and the two tie-in points used for the rope.
Auto-belay use always needs staff permission; staff clip and unclip for the youngest groups.
commonMistakes: Calling a gear loop a place to clip a belay device or auto-belay carabiner — gear loops are not load-bearing.
Skipping the contrast between the belay loop and the tie-in points so later clip-ins go to the wrong point.

progressions.easier: Coach points, kids repeat the names on a harness on the mat.
progressions.harder: Peer callout, then a coach asks ‘show me where the auto-belay clip goes’ and ‘show me where the rope ties in.’

items.name: Clipping Stance Finder
items.setup: Quickdraws on a low bolt board or first bolts of an easy lead line used only for ground/low practice under coach control; or mock-lead setup.
steps: Before clipping, set feet and a solid hand so the clip hand is free.
Practise clipping from that stance with either hand; reset if the body barn-doors.
Name a “good” and “stretched” clip stance on the same bolt.
items.why: Climb’s clipping block and SNCS Level 2 both emphasize finding a stable clipping position before the rope goes near the draw—rushing clips causes errors.
items.variations: Ages 12+: on mock lead with top-rope backup.
items.risk: No live leading until certified. Coach checks every practice clip pattern.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only. Before clipping, set the feet and a solid hand so the clip hand is free.
Practise the clip from that stance with either hand, and reset if the body barn-doors.
Name a ‘good’ stance and a ‘stretched’ stance on the same bolt so the contrast is obvious.
commonMistakes: Rushing the rope toward the draw before the feet are set.
Practising on a live lead before certification; this drill stays on a board, low bolts, or mock lead with a backup.

progressions.easier: Ground or low bolt board, both hands, unhurried.
progressions.harder: Mock lead with a top-rope or auto-belay backup (staff permission for any auto-belay use).

equipment: Quickdraws on a low bolt board or first bolts of an easy line under coach control

images.alt: Lead climber on an indoor wall clipping a quickdraw from a standing stance, with large volumes visible on the wall. Teaching context for Ages 12+ and 14+ only.

items.name: Back-Clip Spotting Board
items.setup: Ground clipping board with several draws; coach presets a mix of correct clips and back-clips.
steps: Climbers walk the board and mark each clip correct or back-clipped.
For each back-clip, explain the rope path (rope should run from the wall/bolt side out toward the climber in the gym’s taught orientation) and fix it.
Retest with new presets.
items.why: Back-clipping is a named failure mode in Climb’s syllabus, GVSU lead objectives, Mazamas sport leader day 2, and SNCS Level 2 assessment standards.
items.variations: Ages 14+: timed personal accuracy set—count your own correct fixes, not against peers.
items.risk: Ground practice only. Agree the gym’s rope-direction teaching model before debating edge cases.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, on the ground. Walk the board and mark each clip correct or back-clipped.
For each back-clip, explain the rope path — the rope should run in the gym’s taught orientation, typically from the wall or bolt side out toward the climber — and fix it.
Agree the gym’s rope-direction model before debating edge cases.
commonMistakes: Calling a clip ‘fine’ without tracing the rope path.
Arguing about rare edge cases before the standard gym orientation is automatic.

progressions.easier: Obvious, exaggerated back-clips mixed with correct clips.
progressions.harder: A personal accuracy set: count your own correct fixes, not against peers.

equipment: Ground clipping board with several draws

images.alt: Quickdraws used on a spotting board to practise recognizing a correct clip and a back-clip.

items.name: Z-Clip Recognition Drill
items.setup: Two draws on a board or low wall; coach demos grabbing rope from below the last clip.
steps: Demo a correct clip: rope taken from near the harness/knot side above the last clipped draw.
Demo a Z-clip: rope taken from below the previous draw into the next, making a Z and heavy drag.
Climbers practise the correct hand path slowly, then identify coach-made Z mistakes.
items.why: Z-clipping is called out across lead syllabi (Climb, Camp5 Lead Wall Course, SNCS) because it creates drag and a hazardous rope path.
items.variations: Start exaggerated and slow. Later, add the cue “grab rope close to the knot.”
items.risk: Ground or mock-lead only. Fix any Z before anyone climbs higher in a mock setting.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, on a board or low wall. A correct clip takes rope from near the harness or knot, above the last clipped draw.
A Z-clip takes rope from below the previous draw into the next, making a Z and heavy drag. Climbers practise the correct hand path, then identify coach-made Z mistakes.
Cue: grab rope close to the knot. Fix any Z before anyone climbs higher in a mock setting.
commonMistakes: Grabbing a loop of rope from below the last draw because it is the closest strand.
Leaving a Z in place and continuing up on mock lead.

progressions.easier: Exaggerated, slow demos on a two-draw board.
progressions.harder: Faster identification of coach-set mistakes, still on the ground or on mock lead with a backup.

equipment: Two quickdraws on a board or low wall

images.alt: Several quickdraws — two carabiners joined by a semi-rigid sling — the gear this drill uses to show a correct rope path and a Z-clip.

items.name: Rope-Behind-Leg Awareness
items.setup: Mock-lead or low lead practice with top-rope backup; coach watches rope and legs.
steps: Climb a few moves with a trailing rope and notice when the rope runs behind a leg or thigh.
Practise moving the rope in front of the legs before the next clip.
Talk through what a fall with the rope behind the leg can do (flip potential) in age-appropriate words.
items.why: Climb’s clipping block explicitly asks “what happens when you put your leg behind the rope?”—a standard lead risk-management teaching point.
items.variations: Demo on the ground with a rope around a volunteer’s leg (gentle, no pulling). On mock lead, coach calls “rope” when it drifts behind a leg.
items.risk: Mock lead / top-rope backup until lead certified. Coach present.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, on mock lead or low lead practice with a top-rope backup. Notice when the trailing rope runs behind a leg or thigh, and move it in front before the next clip.
Talk through, in age-appropriate words, how a fall with the rope behind the leg can flip the climber. A coach can call ‘rope’ when it drifts.
A gentle ground demo with a rope around a volunteer’s leg (no pulling) can make the path visible before the climb.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the rope until after the next clip, or practising this without a real backup belay.
A forceful demo that pulls on a rope wrapped around someone’s leg.

progressions.easier: Ground demo, then a few mock-lead moves with a coach calling ‘rope.’
progressions.harder: The climber self-notices and corrects before each clip, still on a checked backup until lead-certified.

equipment: Mock-lead or low lead practice with top-rope backup

items.name: Rope-Drag Zigzag Demo
items.setup: Mock-lead draws that can be clipped in a zigzag and a straighter line; climbers feel pull by hand on the ground first.
steps: Clip a zigzag path on the board or mock draws and pull rope through—notice the drag.
Reclip a straighter path and compare the pull.
On an easy mock lead, choose draws that keep the rope closer to a straight line when the route allows.
items.why: Rope drag from zigzags is a core lead efficiency and risk topic in lead courses and matches the existing Rope Drag vocabulary already in the library.
items.variations: Ground pulls only for a first session. Later: extend with quickdraw gate orientation so the rope runs clean.
items.risk: Practice under coach control. Do not fight extreme drag by yanking—fix and reclimb the clip plan.

items.name: Gate Orientation Drill
items.setup: Loose quickdraws and a bolt hanger board.
steps: Show dogbone, bolt-end carabiner, rope-end carabiner.
Hang draws so gates face away from the likely fall / travel direction per gym teaching (often alternating or gate away from expected movement).
Climbers hang a set of draws and a partner checks gate direction before any rope is introduced.
items.why: SNCS Level 2 and Climb’s quickdraw anatomy blocks treat gate/spine orientation as part of correct protection setup, not a trivia detail.
items.variations: Ages 12+: climbers hang practice draws on a mock route.
items.risk: Practice hardware only. Real lead walls follow gym rules about pre-hung and climber-placed draws.

items.name: First Three Clips Focus
items.setup: Easy lead line with top-rope backup or auto-belay backup per Climb’s mock-lead model; coach belay for first sessions.
steps: Discuss why the first clips matter most for ground-fall risk management.
On mock lead, practise calm, solid clips on bolts 1–3 only, then lower.
Repeat until those three clips look identical and unhurried.
items.why: SNCS and GVSU materials highlight ground-fall risk before enough clips are in; Climb uses auto-belay-backed mock leading on day 1 for exactly this kind of deliberate practice.
items.variations: Use stick-clip for bolt 1 if the gym teaches it. Only advance to higher bolts after low clips are automatic.
items.risk: Backup belay required. No live lead without certification and coach approval. Steep, clean lines preferred.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, on mock lead with a top-rope or auto-belay backup. Discuss why the first clips matter most for ground-fall risk management.
Practise calm, solid clips on bolts 1–3 only, then lower. Repeat until those three clips look identical and unhurried.
Staff permission is required for any auto-belay backup. No live lead without certification and coach approval.
commonMistakes: Rushing the first clips, or continuing up the wall before the low clips are automatic.
Treating the practice rope as the real belay.

progressions.easier: Pre-hung draws, coach belay, stick-clip for bolt 1 if the gym teaches it.
progressions.harder: Advance to higher bolts only after the first three are consistent.

equipment: Easy lead line with top-rope or auto-belay backup

images.alt: Climber clipping an early quickdraw on a lead wall. Use as a clipping-stance picture for Ages 12+ and 14+ mock-lead practice, not as a cue to lead without a backup.

items.name: Mock Lead with Auto-Belay Backup
items.setup: Lead route with an auto-belay (or top rope) as the true belay; a second rope or the lead rope used only to practise clipping draws.
steps: Partner-check the real belay system first (auto-belay or top rope).
Climb while clipping the practice lead rope into draws; coach watches for back-clips, Z-clips, and rope-behind-leg.
At the top or a chosen height, stop, discuss clips, and lower on the real belay.
items.why: Climb’s lead syllabus schedules mock leading on day 1—lead movement with an auto-belay backup—before day 2 live lead and fall practice.
items.variations: Pre-hung draws first (pinkpoint-style practice), then place draws if the gym allows. Add a coach checklist card: gate, direction, Z, legs, stance.
items.risk: The backup system is the real belay—treat it with a full clip-in or top-rope partner check every time. Practice rope is not the catch.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
Auto-Belay Clip-In Routine or top-rope Partner Check
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only. Partner-check the real belay system first — the auto belay (staff permission required) or top rope is the catch; the practice lead rope is not.
Climb while clipping the practice rope into draws. The coach watches for back-clips, Z-clips, and rope behind the leg.
At the top or a chosen height, stop, discuss the clips, and lower on the real belay.
commonMistakes: Skipping the real-system partner check because ‘it’s only mock lead.’
Leaving a back-clip or Z-clip in place and continuing.

progressions.easier: Pre-hung draws (pinkpoint-style practice) with a coach checklist: gate, direction, Z, legs, stance.
progressions.harder: The climber places draws if the gym allows, still lowering on the real belay.

equipment: Lead route with auto-belay or top-rope as the true belay
A second rope for clipping practice

items.name: Lead Fall Below the Draw
items.setup: Steep, clean lead terrain; climber lead-certified or on a clinic rope with instructor belay; start at least ~2 m below a clipped draw; clear fall zone.
steps: From a four-point easy stance below the clipped draw, breathe, make a small upward move, and let go with relaxed arms.
Land with eyes toward the feet/wall, knees soft, feet apart; optional hand on rope near the knot per Rock & Sun cues.
Increase fall length only when climber and coach agree body language still looks relaxed.
items.why: Rock & Sun stage 4 builds lead falling from below the draw before chin-above or feet-above progressions; Camp5 and Climb keep lead fall practice inside structured clinics.
items.variations: Ages 12+: instructor belay first. Ages 14+: peer lead belay only if both passed the gym lead test and a coach supervises.
items.risk: High consequence. Certified lead belayer, coach present, overhanging clear terrain, climber-chosen progress. Stop early if tension or shrieking returns.
prereqs: Clip-and-Let-Go on Top Rope or Progressive Top-Rope Slump

items.name: Soft-Catch Concept Lab
items.setup: Whiteboard or demo rope; no live falls required in the lab itself.
steps: Define a hard catch (sudden stop, belayer static) and a soft catch (belayer moves with the fall / managed slack) in gym-appropriate terms.
Discuss when a soft catch helps (higher lead falls on steep ground) and when it does not (low to the ground, ledges, swinging into hazards).
Role-play the words belayer and climber use before a planned practice fall.
items.why: Climb’s falling discussion and GVSU objectives explicitly contrast soft and hard catches and weight differences before climbers practise catching lead falls.
items.variations: Add a supervised ground-weight demo with a backup belayer if the gym allows. Pair with Lead Fall Below the Draw on a later day—not the same hour for brand-new belayers.
items.risk: Concepts first; live soft catches only with certified lead belayers under coach oversight.
coachingCues: Ages 12+ and 14+ only. Define a hard catch (sudden stop, belayer static) and a soft catch (belayer moves with the fall, or managed slack) in gym-appropriate words — no live falls required in the lab itself.
Discuss when a soft catch can help (higher lead falls on steep ground) and when it does not (low to the ground, ledges, swinging into hazards).
Role-play the words belayer and climber use before a planned practice fall. Live soft catches come later, only with certified lead belayers under coach oversight.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to a live lead fall on the same day the idea is introduced.
Treating a soft catch as ‘give a big loop of slack’ in a place where a longer fall would hit a ledge or the ground.

progressions.easier: Whiteboard and rope-on-the-ground discussion only.
progressions.harder: A supervised ground-weight demo with a backup, if the gym allows, then a later planned fall session — not the same hour for brand-new belayers.

equipment: No live falls required in the lab

items.name: Lead Age-Readiness Talk
items.setup: Seated group; gym lead policy printed or summarized by coach.
steps: Review common prerequisites from published courses: solid top-rope belay, comfortable moderate top-rope climbing, minimum ages often ~12–13 (some programs 10–12 only with a participating adult).
Each climber writes two skills they already have and one they still need (clipping, falling comfort, belay stance, endurance).
Set a process goal for the block—not a deadline to “get lead card.”
items.why: Published lead courses set age and skill gates (often about 12–13+). A short readiness talk keeps ages 9–12 honest about waiting, and helps ages 12+ / 14+ map the gym’s real prerequisites without rushing into lead.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: readiness talk only—no mock lead or live lead; focus on what still needs practice on top rope. Ages 12+ and Ages 14+: map the gym lead-test rubric and set process goals. Ages 14+: map the gym’s exact test rubric.
items.risk: Do not pressure early lead. Gym policy always comes first over any curriculum sample.

items.name: Commands Clarity Ladder
items.setup: Pairs across a noisy gym space but still able to hear; no climbing required.
steps: Caller says a command at conversation volume; partner echoes the exact gym response.
Increase distance step by step, keeping words crisp—not shouted garbage.
Finish with the full start-up chain and the take/lower chain.
items.why: Clear commands are required in Climb’s belay protocols and SNCS assessment standards; practising clarity away from the wall prevents mumbled calls on real climbs.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 4–6: two-word gym baby commands only. Ages 12+: add lead calls (slack, clipping, falling).
items.risk: Use only the gym’s command set so class words match floor staff.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays
coachingCues: Use only the gym’s command set. The caller speaks at conversation volume; the partner echoes the exact gym response.
Increase distance step by step, keeping words crisp — not shouted mush — and finish with the full start-up chain and the take/lower chain.
If the drill is paired with auto-belay practice, staff permission is still required before anyone uses a device.
commonMistakes: Inventing alternate words that do not match floor staff.
Shouting unintelligible calls, or skipping the partner’s reply.

progressions.easier: Pairs close together, start-up commands only.
progressions.harder: More distance in a noisy gym, then the full take/lower chain.

equipment: Open floor space still within hearing

items.name: Partner Check Point-Trace
items.setup: Belay pairs fully dressed to climb; coach watches one pair at a time.
steps: Checker points to and says: harness buckles, figure-8 through both tie-ins and dressed, belay device on belay loop, locker locked, rope-end knot if required, loose clothing/hair clear.
Swap roles. Climber does not pull on until both have finished.
Coach asks one surprise question (“show me the brake strand”) before go.
items.why: Extends the existing Partner Check habit with a mandatory point-and-trace motor pattern; Climb and ABC both stress that checks fail when they become waved gestures.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: fewer items, coach completes the list. Lead day add-ons: backup knot, lead end identified, draws racked.
items.risk: No check, no climb. Uncertified belayers always have a staff backup.
coachingCues: The checker points to and says each item: harness buckles, figure-8 through both tie-ins and dressed, device on the belay loop, locker locked, rope-end knot if required, loose clothing and hair clear.
Swap roles. The climber does not pull on until both have finished. A coach can ask one surprise question (‘show me the brake strand’) before go.
No check, no climb. Uncertified belayers always have a staff backup.
commonMistakes: Waving a hand over the system without touching or naming each point.
Starting to climb when only one person has finished the check.

progressions.easier: A shorter list for Ages 6–9, with the coach completing the remaining items.
progressions.harder: On a later Ages 12+ or 14+ lead day, add backup knot, lead end identified, and draws racked.

items.name: Paying Out and Taking In
items.setup: Ground school with a moving partner walking away/toward the belayer; backup belayer; gym-approved device.
steps: As the partner walks away, pay out smooth slack without locking the device early (especially ABD/Grigri awareness).
As the partner walks in, take in quickly while the brake hand stays on the brake strand.
Name errors: short-roping (too tight) and too much slack.
items.why: GVSU and SNCS lead-belay objectives call out smooth slack payout, rapid take-in, and avoiding short-roping or premature ABD lock-up.
items.variations: Tube device and ABD in separate turns if the gym teaches both. Add a sudden sit by the partner (with backup) to practise a catch stance.
items.risk: Backup always. No unsupervised belaying. Device-specific techniques must match staff teaching.
coachingCues: As the partner walks away, pay out smooth slack without locking an assisted-braking device early. As they walk in, take in quickly with the brake hand staying on the brake strand.
Name the errors out loud: short-roping (too tight) and too much slack.
Device-specific technique must match staff teaching. A backup is always present.
commonMistakes: Short-roping a moving partner, or giving a large, unmanaged loop of slack.
Letting the brake hand leave the rope, or fighting an ABD that has locked because payout was jerked.

progressions.easier: Slow walk-away and walk-in on the ground, tube device first if the gym teaches both.
progressions.harder: A sudden sit by the partner (with backup) to practise a catch stance, then ABD payout awareness in a separate turn.

items.name: Top-Rope Endurance Laps
items.setup: Easy top-rope routes well below limit; belay pairs; partner check every relisten/re-tie.
steps: Climb an easy route at a talk pace, lower or downclimb, rest briefly, repeat for a set number of personal laps.
Focus on straight arms, a light grip and resting early rather than grade; keep the pump low, about 1–2 out of 5.
Log your own lap count; try to match it next week with equal or better form.
items.why: Momentum’s two-in-a-rows and disco climbing show how rope volume builds endurance when the grade stays easy and checks stay strict.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: two climbs total. Ages 9–12: disco style to bolt 3, downclimb, repeat. Ages 12+: continuous easy laps with planned rests.
items.risk: Partner check every time someone ties in again. Stop when form breaks. Brake hand rules never relax with fatigue.
coachingCues: Choose climbs well within ability so the athlete can practice pacing, straight arms, and rests rather than fighting a redpoint.
Pump is the forearm getting so full of metabolic waste that even a basic grip is hard; shake out and rest before that happens.
Downclimbing a lap can count as more time on the wall if the belayer is giving working slack.
commonMistakes: Picking a hard project for endurance, which usually becomes a short, intense fight.
The belayer holding the climber tight so the lap is a lower, not a climb.

progressions.easier: One easy top-rope up and down.
progressions.harder: A set of easy laps with a short rest between, or a longer easy route with planned shake-outs.

items.name: Auto-Belay Endurance Colors
items.setup: Easy auto-belay colors; full clip-in routine every lap; coach floor-walking.
steps: Complete the clip-in routine, climb an easy color at pace-control speed, lower, unclip on the ground, rest.
Repeat for a personal target number of quality laps.
If complacency shows (rushed clip), freeze the session and redo the routine slowly.
items.why: TRUBLUE markets auto belays for endurance training, and ABC warns that experienced climbers fail when they rush the clip after many laps—so endurance blocks must keep the routine sacred.
items.variations: Any program age with staff permission to use auto belays. Parent & Child and Ages 3–4: staff clips and unclips; child names steps. Ages 4–6: staff-controlled clip-in until the gym says otherwise. Ages 6–9+: supervised self-clip where policy allows, still with a staff go signal. Ages 6–9: two laps. Ages 12+: longer sets still below pump-out.
items.risk: Full double-check every lap. Staff watch for unclipped starts. No outclimbing retraction.
prereqs: Staff permission to use auto belays

items.name: Quickdraw Anatomy Sort
items.setup: Disassembled practice draws (or labeled photos if hardware cannot be borrowed).
steps: Sort: bolt-end carabiner, rope-end carabiner, dogbone/sewn sling.
Reassemble correctly and explain which end usually has the bent gate in many gym draws.
Partner checks the rebuild.
items.why: Climb’s day-1 gear overview and SNCS equipment blocks require climbers to know draw anatomy before they clip them on lead.
items.variations: Photo cards for gyms that will not hand out loose hardware. Add a worn and retired sling discussion for older teens.
items.risk: Practice gear only; nothing with unknown history goes back on a climb without staff approval.

items.name: Closed-System Rope End
items.setup: Belay ropes with enough end to tie the gym’s required end knot.
steps: Show why a rope-end knot (barrel / double overhand, per gym) stops the rope from running through the device.
Each belayer ties and dresses the end knot, partner checks.
Add the end knot to the partner-check list out loud.
items.why: Partner-check lists in youth programs and lead clinics routinely include the rope-end knot as part of a closed belay system.
items.variations: Some gyms use rope-end bags or sewn ends—teach the local method, not a generic substitute.
items.risk: Follow gym policy exactly. A missing end knot is a no-climb item.
prereqs: Knot Practice or Figure-8 Dressing Lab

items.name: Backup Belayer Habit
items.setup: Top-rope team of three: climber, belayer, backup; coach assigns roles.
steps: Backup stands ready to catch the brake strand without interfering.
Run a short climb with coach watching the belayer’s brake hand and the backup’s attention.
Rotate roles. Only certified or coach-approved belayers take the primary role.
items.why: Ground-school progressions and youth SOPs keep a backup until climbers pass a belay test; the habit belongs in class even after some kids certify.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: backup is always a coach. Ages 12+: trained peers backup under coach eyes.
items.risk: Backup does not mean unsupervised. Gym certification still gates primary belaying.
coachingCues: The backup stands ready to catch the brake strand without interfering with the primary belayer.
Only certified or coach-approved belayers take the primary role; a backup does not mean unsupervised belaying.
For Ages 6–9 the backup is always a coach.
commonMistakes: The backup watching the climber instead of the brake strand, or grabbing the rope in a way that fights the primary.
Treating a peer backup as permission to belay without a coach nearby.

progressions.easier: Coach is the backup on every short climb.
progressions.harder: Trained peers backup under coach eyes after the primary has passed the gym’s belay test.

items.name: Tic Tac Toe Foot Taps
items.setup: A slightly overhanging or vertical wall with two big jugs at a comfortable height and a spread of footholds to each side at knee, hip and head height. Start no higher than a climber can step down from.
steps: Hang from two big jugs with both feet on a starting foothold.
With the right foot, reach out and tap a foothold far to the right at knee height, then bring the foot back to the start hold.
Repeat to the right at hip height, then at head height, moving the hips each time, not just the leg.
Switch to the left foot and work back down: head height, hip height, knee height, returning to the start hold after each tap.
Step down, rest, and swap turns.
items.why: The book uses this as wall-based core activation: reaching a foot out wide while hanging makes the trunk work to keep the body on the wall. It previews the body tension a steep problem needs.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: vertical wall, closer footholds, knee and hip height only. Ages 12+ and 14+: steeper wall, wider and higher taps. Use it as the first part of a body-tension or steep-wall skill block.
items.risk: Big jugs only; this is about the trunk, not the fingers. Stop the set if a climber is pulling with bent, shaking arms or the feet keep slipping. Low starts only, with a clear fall zone and pads.
coachingCues: Move the hips toward the foot you're reaching with.
Quiet tap, then back to the start foothold.
Arms long; the trunk does the work.
commonMistakes: Reaching only with the leg while the hips stay stuck.
Going on a small or slippery start hold so the hands overgrip.

progressions.easier: Vertical wall, closer footholds, only two heights.
progressions.harder: Steeper wall and wider foot targets; hold each tap for a second before returning.

items.name: Diagonal Hang
items.setup: A steep wall with big jugs and big footholds low enough that the climber can step off. Each climber picks one jug and a foothold diagonally across from it.
steps: Start with both hands on big jugs and both feet on footholds.
Let go with one hand and lift the foot on the same side, so only one hand and the opposite foot stay on.
Hold the diagonal for 5–10 seconds with a long arm and tight trunk.
Put the hand and foot back, rest, and repeat on the other diagonal.
items.why: The book's diagonal hang trains full-body tension along the cross-body line a climber uses on steep ground. It is a core and shoulder drill on the wall, not a grip test.
items.variations: Ages 12+: close hand and foot, 5 seconds. Ages 14+: move the foot farther away, or hold up to about 10 seconds. The book allows 10–15 seconds; we keep holds shorter for youth.
items.risk: Jugs only, never edges. Short holds with full rest. Keep the shoulder engaged (pulled slightly down) rather than hanging off the joint. Skip it for anyone with shoulder pain.
coachingCues: Long arm, shoulder pulled down.
Squeeze the trunk so the hip stays close to the wall.
Breathe through the hold.
commonMistakes: Shrugging up into the ear on the hanging arm.
Twisting the hips away from the wall so the body swings open (barn-door).

progressions.easier: Keep both feet on and lift only one hand.
progressions.harder: Spread the hand and foot farther apart.

items.name: Swing to Stick
items.setup: A steep wall with a big jug that can be reached from the start footholds, and several footholds at different distances. Pads under the whole swing zone.
steps: Start in balance on the start footholds, holding the big jug with both hands.
Let the feet come off in control so the body hangs on straight arms.
As the swing comes back toward the wall, place both feet onto a chosen foothold and hold the position for two seconds.
Step down, rest, and pick a foothold a little farther away next time.
items.why: This is the book's swing-and-stick body-tension drill, adapted: climbers learn to bring the feet back on after cutting loose, a key steep-wall skill. Starting from the wall replaces the book's jump start.
items.variations: Ages 12+: closest footholds, no hold on the swing. Ages 14+: farther footholds, then one foot only. No jumping or running starts at any age.
items.risk: No jump starts and no running starts. Jugs only. Clear fall zone; one climber at a time on each section. Stop if the hands are slipping or the shoulders hurt.
coachingCues: Straight arms, let the swing settle.
Toes pull in; drive the feet onto the hold.
Freeze, then breathe.
commonMistakes: Pulling up on bent arms instead of swinging the feet.
Kicking at the wall instead of placing the foot.

progressions.easier: Keep one foot on the wall and swing only the other foot back on.
progressions.harder: Pick a farther or smaller foothold, or stick it with one foot.

equipment: Steep wall with a big jug

items.name: Band-Resisted Traverse
items.setup: A low, easy traverse with feet no higher than about knee height and pads underneath. A long, light resistance band loops around the climber's hips; a partner on the ground holds the other end.
steps: The partner stands behind the climber and holds the band with light, steady tension.
The climber traverses slowly, keeping the hips close to the wall against the gentle pull.
The partner walks along and keeps the pull smooth and light; no sudden yanks.
After one length, swap roles.
items.why: The book suggests traversing with a band pulling on the hips or a foot to make the trunk and feet work harder. A gentle pull teaches climbers to keep tension and keep the feet loaded.
items.variations: Ages 12+: band on the hips, very light. Ages 14+: try the band on one foot to make that foot work harder. The coach can hold the band for climbers new to it.
items.risk: Light band and gentle pull only, never a tug-of-war. Feet stay low. The partner keeps the band below hip height, pulls away from the wall only, and lets go if the climber says stop. Agree on a word for stop before starting.
coachingCues: Hips in, feet pressing.
Partner: smooth and light.
Talk: say 'more' or 'less'.
commonMistakes: Partner yanking or pulling upward.
Climber leaning back and hanging off straight arms with hips away from the wall.

progressions.easier: Coach holds the band; just a few moves.
progressions.harder: Band on one foot, or a slightly steeper traverse.

items.name: Rest-Hold Ladder
items.setup: An easy, non-overhanging traverse or low boulder circuit with a few big jugs marked as rest stations.
steps: Climb easy holds until the forearms feel a slight pump, well before they are tired.
Stop on a marked jug, take one hand off and let it hang loose for a few seconds while breathing slowly.
Swap hands when the holding hand starts to tire. Aim for four or five swaps, with each hand resting about 3–10 seconds.
When the arms feel fresh again, leave the rest and keep climbing. Over the weeks, move to steeper climbing with rests on vertical jugs, then steep climbing with steep rests.
items.why: The book lays out this exact progression for learning to recover on the wall, and notes that most new climbers never think to rest until they are already fully pumped. It turns resting into a skill climbers practise.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: vertical wall only, with coach counting the swaps. Ages 12+ and 14+: progress to steep climbing between rests, then rests on steep walls. Top-rope groups can use the same idea on a route.
items.risk: Stop well before a full pump. Jugs only for rests. Keep traverses low or use top-rope with a checked belay.
coachingCues: Rest early, not late.
Loose hand, long breath out.
Swap before the holding hand tires.
commonMistakes: Waiting until fully pumped before resting.
Rushing the swaps or holding the breath.

progressions.easier: Vertical wall, three swaps, coach counts.
progressions.harder: Steep climbing between rests, then rests on a steep wall.

items.name: Crux-and-Traverse Intervals
items.setup: One long, very easy traverse, plus two or three short boulder problems near it that are hard but doable for each climber (4–8 moves). Write the circuit on a whiteboard.
steps: Traverse easily for about 2 minutes.
Step off and try a short hard problem once, with full effort and good form.
Go straight back on the easy traverse until the arms feel less pumped (about 1–3 minutes).
Repeat for two or three hard problems, ending with a few minutes of easy traversing. Stop the circuit early if a climber gets fully pumped.
items.why: The book prefers this to the classic 4x4 that ends in a total pump: short hard efforts, like the crux of a route, separated by easy climbing so the forearms can flush and re-oxygenate. A study it reports found easy traversing between attempts helped the final attempt more than walking.
items.variations: Ages 12+: one round with two hard problems. Ages 14+: two rounds, or a longer middle problem. Rate the pump after each traverse on a 1–5 scale and keep it at 3 or below.
items.risk: Problems hard but not limit; no tiny crimps or monos. Stop if form breaks down or the pump will not drop on the traverse. Not for climbers returning from finger pain.
coachingCues: Hard problem: crisp and committed.
Traverse: softest grip, slow breathing.
Back on the hard problem only when the pump drops.
commonMistakes: Turning the traverse into a hard climb.
Pushing on to a full pump on the hard problem.

progressions.easier: Use only one hard problem, or make it a few moves easier.
progressions.harder: Add a second round, or move the hard problems onto steeper terrain.

items.name: Pump-Check Timer Laps
items.setup: An easy traverse or set of easy boulders, a stopwatch per pair, and a 1–5 pump scale on the whiteboard (1 = fresh, 5 = can't hold on).
steps: Pick a target climbing time (start with 4 minutes for younger groups, up to 8 for teens).
Start the watch when the climber gets on. Climb easy holds with a light grip.
When the pump goes above 2 out of 5, step off and pause the watch.
Rest as long as needed, get back on and restart the watch. Finish when the climbing time adds up to the target.
items.why: This is the book's intermittent endurance method for less experienced climbers. Keeping the pump low (about 1–2 out of 5) keeps blood flowing in the forearms. That is what builds the capillaries behind endurance, and climbers learn to read their own effort.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: 4 minutes, partner runs the watch. Ages 12+: 6 minutes. Ages 14+: 8 minutes or two blocks. Top-rope groups can do the same on easy routes.
items.risk: Easy holds only, no crimps. Climbers stop themselves at 2 out of 5; coach checks honest ratings. Low traverses or checked top-rope belays.
coachingCues: Light grip; let the feet carry the weight.
Check your number every few moves.
Off at 2, on when fresh.
commonMistakes: Pushing past 2 to get more time on the watch.
Climbing holds that are too hard for an endurance lap.

progressions.easier: Shorter target time; partner calls out pump checks.
progressions.harder: Longer target, slightly steeper wall, same easy holds.

items.name: Glute Bridge
items.setup: Mats or floor space away from the walls.
steps: Lie on the back with knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart.
Squeeze the bottom muscles and lift the hips until shoulders, hips and knees form a straight line.
Stop there; don't arch the lower back higher.
Hold for a breath and lower slowly. Do 6–10.
items.why: The book recommends the glute bridge over lower-back extensions. It trains the glutes, hamstrings and lower back to work together, the same push that stands a climber up on a high foot.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: 6 slow reps, coach checks the straight line. Ages 9–12: add a 2-second pause at the top. Ages 12+ and 14+: single-leg bridges.
items.risk: Stop at the straight line; no over-arching. Skip it for anyone with back pain.
coachingCues: Push through the heels.
Squeeze the bottom, not the back.
Straight line from knees to shoulders.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to lift higher.
Pushing through the toes so the thighs do the work.

progressions.easier: Smaller lift and fewer reps.
progressions.harder: Single-leg bridge, or a short pause at the top.

items.name: Cat-Cow
items.setup: Mats or floor space; climbers on hands and knees.
steps: On hands and knees, hands under shoulders, knees under hips.
Cow: let the belly drop, lift the chin and squeeze the shoulder blades together.
Cat: tuck the chin, push the floor away and round the back up like a grumpy cat.
Move slowly between the two, about 5–8 times, with a breath each way.
items.why: The book lists cat-cow as a mobility exercise for the spine. For young climbers it is a simple active movement that wakes up the back and shoulders without any held stretch.
items.variations: Ages 3–4 and 4–6: add the animal sound (cat, cow). Ages 6–9+: add a pause at each end. Ages 12+: link it to shoulder-blade control.
items.risk: Slow and comfortable; no forcing the range. Skip it for any back or wrist pain.
coachingCues: Slow, with a breath each way.
Move the whole back, not just the neck.
Push the floor away on the cat.
commonMistakes: Moving fast and flopping.
Only moving the head.

progressions.easier: Smaller movements, coach demonstrates alongside.
progressions.harder: Add a pause at each end and match it to the breath.

items.name: Pallof Press
items.setup: A light resistance band anchored at chest height to a fixed point away from the climbing walls, or held by a partner standing to the side.
steps: Stand side-on to the anchor, feet about hip-width, knees soft.
Hold the band at the chest with both hands, shoulders down, head in line.
Press the hands straight out in front and hold for a breath without letting the band twist you.
Bring the hands back to the chest. Do 6–8, then face the other way.
items.why: The book uses this anti-rotation exercise because the trunk muscles stopping the twist are the same ones that stop a barn-door swing on the wall.
items.variations: Ages 12+: light band, wide stance. Ages 14+: narrower stance or a slightly stronger band.
items.risk: Light band only. Anchor firmly or use a coach as the partner. Stop if the lower back aches.
coachingCues: Press straight out; don't let it turn you.
Ribs down, shoulders down.
Breathe out as you press.
commonMistakes: Twisting toward the anchor.
Locked knees and arched lower back.

progressions.easier: Wider stance and lighter band.
progressions.harder: Narrower stance, or a slow press and hold.

items.name: Box Step-Ups
items.setup: A sturdy, non-slip box or bench that won't tip, at about knee height, away from the walls.
steps: Put one whole foot on the box.
Push through that foot and stand all the way up; bring the other foot up for a light tap on the box.
Lower slowly back down with the same leg doing the work.
Do 6–8 per leg.
items.why: The book rates the step-up as a strong match for climbing, especially for pushing up off a very high foothold. A higher step works the glutes more.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: low box, bodyweight only. Ages 12+ and 14+: higher box or a slow lowering. Link it to High Step drills on the wall.
items.risk: Bodyweight only. Box must be stable and non-slip. Stop if a knee hurts.
coachingCues: Push with the top leg, not a bounce off the bottom.
Knee in line with the toes.
Lower slowly.
commonMistakes: Jumping off the bottom foot.
Letting the knee collapse inward.

progressions.easier: Lower box and a hand on a wall for balance.
progressions.harder: Higher box, or a slow three-count lowering.

items.name: Bench Pistol Progression
items.setup: A sturdy bench or box behind each climber, away from the walls.
steps: Stand on one leg in front of the bench.
Lower slowly on that leg until seated on the bench.
Put both feet down to stand up again (week 1), or stand up on the one leg once that feels steady.
Do 4–6 per leg. Over weeks, use a lower bench.
items.why: The book builds toward a single-leg squat by sitting down onto a bench, then standing back up, then gradually lowering the bench. It builds the one-leg strength used on rock-overs and high steps.
items.variations: Ages 12+: seated lowering only. Ages 14+: stand back up on one leg, then a lower bench.
items.risk: Bodyweight only. Controlled speed. Stop if the knee hurts or drifts inward.
coachingCues: Slow on the way down.
Knee tracks over the toes.
Arms forward for balance.
commonMistakes: Dropping onto the bench.
Knee collapsing inward.

progressions.easier: Higher bench, both feet to stand.
progressions.harder: Lower bench, stand up on one leg.

items.name: Pull-Up Lowering
items.setup: A pull-up bar or big jugs on a board, with a sturdy step so the climber can start at the top without pulling.
steps: Use the step to get the chin over the bar (or chest to the jugs).
Set the shoulders down and back.
Lower slowly, about 3 seconds, to straight but soft arms.
Step back up rather than pulling. Do 3–5, with a full rest between sets.
items.why: The book calls lowering the most efficient way to work toward a first full pull-up, because muscles produce more force while lengthening. It also reminds climbers to set the shoulder blades first.
items.variations: Ages 12+: 3 reps, coach checks shoulder position. Ages 14+: up to 5 reps or a pause halfway. Bodyweight only at every age; the book's added-weight step is not used here.
items.risk: Bodyweight only, bar or big jugs only. No edges and no added weight. Stop if elbows or shoulders hurt.
coachingCues: Shoulders down before you lower.
Slow and even all the way.
Soft elbows at the bottom.
commonMistakes: Dropping fast in the last half.
Shrugging up into the ears.

progressions.easier: Lower from halfway, or use feet on a box for part of the weight.
progressions.harder: Slower lowering or a pause halfway.

items.name: Contract-Relax Hamstring Stretch
items.setup: Home or non-climbing-day mobility. A mat and a long strap or towel.
steps: Lie on the back, strap around one foot, leg raised until a light stretch.
Gently press the heel down into the strap for 10–15 seconds without moving the leg.
Relax, then ease the leg a little higher and hold the light stretch for 15–20 seconds.
Do 2–4 rounds per leg.
items.why: The book describes this contract-relax method for longer-term range work and reports that it gains more range than passive stretching. It is kept away from climbing sessions because long stretches before climbing reduce strength for a while.
items.variations: Ages 12+: two rounds per leg, with coach demonstrating. Ages 14+: up to four rounds. Not used in class warm-ups.
items.risk: Light stretch only, no pain and no bouncing. Not on climbing days and never before climbing.
coachingCues: Light stretch, not a pull.
Press gently, don't move.
Breathe out as you ease further.
commonMistakes: Pushing into pain.
Doing it right before climbing.

progressions.easier: Smaller range, two rounds.
progressions.harder: Add a short squeeze of the front of the thigh before easing further.

items.name: Foam Roll Primer
items.setup: Foam rollers or massage balls, laid out away from the walls.
steps: Pick one stiff area: calves, hamstrings, glutes or upper back.
Roll slowly over it, 8–10 passes, with easy pressure.
Straight away, try the movement you want (a high step or deep squat) to feel the range.
Move on to the warm-up.
items.why: The book suggests about 8–10 passes with a roller or ball to calm the signals that limit range, so a climber can then move more freely. It's a quick option before an active warm-up, not a replacement for it.
items.variations: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, optional, before class or as part of home mobility. Keep it to 2–3 minutes inside the group's warm-up.
items.risk: Easy pressure. No rolling on joints, the lower back, the neck or any injury. Stop if it is painful.
coachingCues: Slow passes, easy pressure.
One area, then test it.
Breathe.
commonMistakes: Rolling fast and hard.
Rolling on a sore joint or the lower back.

progressions.easier: Use a softer roller or a ball against the wall.
progressions.harder: Pair it with an active range drill right after.

items.name: Rebuild the Move
items.setup: Any move a climber has become nervous about after a slip, a scare or a tweak, set low on an easy boulder. The climber chooses each step.
steps: Talk through the move together, then picture it once with eyes closed.
Do the smallest piece of it from the ground: just place the foot, or just reach to the hold.
Add one piece at a time only when the last one felt easy, with a slow breath before each try.
Finish when the climber feels ready to stop. Name what went well.
items.why: The book explains that the brain tightens up around a move it links with harm, even after the body has healed, and that good, controlled experiences loosen that brake. Rebuilding in small, successful steps gives the brain new evidence.
items.variations: Ages 6–9: coach picks a very small first step and plenty of praise. Ages 9–12+: climber plans the steps on a whiteboard. Teens: link it to visualization and breathing.
items.risk: Climber sets the pace and can stop any time. Low moves over pads. Any real pain means a check with a parent or medical professional first.
coachingCues: Smallest piece first.
Breathe, then go.
You choose the next step.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to the full move.
Coach pushing for height or speed.

progressions.easier: Stay on the first one or two pieces for the session.
progressions.harder: Do the full move, then try it in a short sequence.

items.name: Band Face Pulls
items.setup: Light resistance bands anchored between chest and head height, away from the climbing walls. After climbing.
steps: Hold the band with both hands, arms forward, palms down.
Pull the band toward the face, elbows high and wide, hands moving apart.
At the end, pinch the shoulder blades together and keep the shoulders down.
Return slowly. Do 8–12.
items.why: The book picks face pulls for the upper back and the muscles that rotate the shoulder outward, which climbing under-uses. Training them balances all the pulling. It notes they belong after climbing, as strength work, not in the warm-up.
items.variations: Ages 12+: light band, 8 reps. Ages 14+: up to 12 reps or two sets. Pair with Band Pull-Aparts and Wall Angel Hold.
items.risk: Light band. Anchor firmly. Not in the warm-up, so the shoulder muscles aren't tired before climbing. Stop for any shoulder pain.
coachingCues: Elbows high, hands apart.
Squeeze the shoulder blades, shoulders down.
Slow on the way back.
commonMistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up.
Using a band so strong the back arches.

progressions.easier: Lighter band and fewer reps.
progressions.harder: Add a short pause with the hands apart.

items.name: Ramp-Up Boulders
items.setup: Three or four boulders that preview the day's skill, set or picked from easiest to hardest, all on big, open holds. This is the last part of the warm-up for Ages 9–12, 12+ and 14+, after the pulse raiser, active mobility and activation.
steps: Climb the easiest boulder, smoothly, using the day's target skill.
Move to the next one up, still on big holds.
Keep climbing up the ladder, adding a bigger move or a steeper angle each time, but no small crimps yet.
Only after the ladder go on to the main block, small holds or harder problems.
items.why: The book wants the wall part of the warm-up to match the session (bigger moves before a dynamic day, for example) and links pulley injuries to crimping without enough easy climbing first. For the older groups it closes the warm-up, so a good number of easy, progressive moves (the book cites research asking for about 100) come before any crimping.
items.variations: Ages 9–12: about 6 minutes, three boulders. Ages 12+: about 7 minutes, four boulders. Ages 14+: about 9 minutes, four or five boulders, working toward about 100 easy moves before small edges. Match the ladder to the day (steep, dynamic, slab).
items.risk: Big holds only on the ladder. Nobody goes to small crimps or limit moves before finishing it.
coachingCues: Easy and smooth first.
Each climb a little bigger, not smaller holds.
Preview today's skill.
commonMistakes: Skipping straight to the hardest problem.
Choosing crimpy problems for the ramp.

progressions.easier: Two easy boulders and a coach demo.
progressions.harder: Add a steep or dynamic boulder at the top of the ladder.

items.name: Three-Pad Edge Hang
items.setup: A fingerboard (hangboard) with a 24 mm, three-pad edge, or an equally deep three-pad hold, mounted so the climber can step on and off from a box. Only after the session's full warm-up and Ramp-Up Boulders, inside the main block.
steps: Check in: no finger pain today, warm-up and ramp-up done.
Step up to the 24 mm three-pad edge with an open hand (or half crimp), all four fingers on, thumb off; never a full crimp.
Shoulder blades back and down, arms straight with soft elbows, head in line, wrists straight. Lift the feet off the box.
Hang about 7–10 seconds and step down while at least 5 more seconds would still be easy. Rest about 3 minutes.
Repeat, building the total hang time across the session toward about 1 minute 30 seconds over several weeks. Log the total and how hard it felt.
items.why: The book gives bar hangs and hangs on a 24 mm edge or three-pad fingerboard hold as the finger-strength options for climbers under 16 or with little systematic training, in place of maximal protocols. Its novice plan moves from bar hangs to three-pad fingerboard hangs, aiming for about 1 min 30 s. Strength comes mainly from better nervous-system recruitment, so short, good-quality hangs with full rest suit this age.
items.variations: Ages 12+: start with feet lightly on the box to take some weight, then full hangs; hang time stays short with plenty in reserve. Ages 14+: full bodyweight hangs and a larger total. This program sets the hang length, the 5-second reserve and the rest; the book gives the edge size, the target total and the technique. No smaller edges, added weight, one-arm, repeater or campus work at either age before about 16.
items.risk: Ages 12+ and 14+ only, with a coach present. 24 mm three-pad edge only; no small edges, no added weight, no one-arm, repeater or maximal hangs before about 16. Never at the start of a session: only after the full warm-up and ramp-up. At most twice a week, with at least a day between. Stop at any finger, elbow or shoulder pain and tell a coach and parent.
prereqs: About six weeks of Dead Hang (bar hang) work, with 1–1.5 minutes of total hang time feeling comfortable
At least a season of regular climbing in this program (the book's own novice plan spends about four months on general preparation first)
Full warm-up and Ramp-Up Boulders completed this session
No current finger pain; coach present
coachingCues: Open hand, four fingers, no thumb wrap.
Shoulders down and back; straight, soft arms.
Step down with time in reserve.
commonMistakes: Hanging to failure or until the fingers open.
Shrugging up into the ears or bending the wrists.

progressions.easier: Feet lightly on the box, or go back to Dead Hang (bar) for another week.
progressions.harder: Ages 14+: slightly longer hangs, still stopping with 5 seconds in reserve; never a smaller edge or added weight.

equipment: Fingerboard with a 24 mm three-pad edge
